teile.einleitung: Neutrality means that a state does not take part in wars between other states. Switzerland has been neutral for more than 200 years, and this stance is one of its best-known features. But exactly what neutrality requires is still debated again and again today.
wichtigste: Switzerland does not take part in wars between other states.
After the defeat at Marignano in 1515, the Confederation withdrew from the wars of the great powers.
At the Congress of Vienna and in the Second Peace of Paris in 1815, permanent neutrality was recognised.
The Hague Convention of 1907 sets out the law of neutrality in land warfare.
Switzerland defends its neutrality with its own army; this is called armed neutrality.
Neutral Switzerland is not a member of NATO.
With its good offices, Switzerland mediates between states.

abschnitte.text: A **neutral state** does not fight in other countries’ wars and does not support any side in a war with soldiers. It may not belong to any military alliance that would commit it to a war. That is why Switzerland is not a member of **NATO**. Besides Switzerland, Austria and Ireland, for example, are also neutral. Switzerland is, however, a member of the UN, because that is compatible with neutrality.

In 1515 the Confederates lost the Battle of **Marignano** in Italy against France. After that they kept out of the great wars of Europe. Many Swiss, however, continued to fight as mercenaries in foreign armies. In 1815, at the **Congress of Vienna** and in the Second Peace of Paris, the great powers recognised Switzerland’s permanent neutrality. Since then Switzerland has not fought a war against another country.

The **law of neutrality** sets out the duties a neutral state has, for example in the Hague Convention of 1907. A neutral state may not favour any side in a war and may not make its territory available for the purposes of war. **Neutrality policy**, by contrast, covers voluntary measures with which a state makes its neutrality credible. From 1920 to 1938, as a member of the League of Nations, Switzerland practised differential neutrality and took part in economic sanctions. After that it returned to full, integral neutrality.

Switzerland defends its neutrality with its own **army**, which is why people speak of armed neutrality. During both world wars the army was mobilised to protect the borders. In the Second World War Switzerland was completely surrounded by powers at war. Later it was criticised for having done business with Nazi Germany and for turning away many refugees. In 1996 Switzerland joined NATO’s **Partnership for Peace** without becoming a member.

Neutral Switzerland offers other states its **good offices**. It mediates in conflicts and organises peace talks, often in Geneva. It also takes on **protecting power mandates**, which means it represents the interests of one country in another country when the two have no direct relations. Since 1980, for example, Switzerland has represented the interests of the USA in Iran.

In February 2022, after the Russian attack on Ukraine, the Federal Council adopted the EU’s **sanctions** against Russia. This sparked a broad debate about how neutral Switzerland still is. Some think Switzerland must clearly take the side of the country that was attacked. Others want to interpret neutrality as strictly as possible and set it out more precisely in the constitution.

begriffe.erklaerung: The stance of a state not to take part in wars between other states.
Penalties against a country, for example a ban on trade.
A soldier who fights for a foreign country in return for pay.
A country that represents the interests of another country when that country has no embassy there.

gewusst: The Swiss Guard in the Vatican is still a reminder today of the time when Swiss men served as mercenaries in foreign service.
At times Switzerland had so many protecting power mandates that during the Second World War it represented the interests of more than 30 states.
The word neutral comes from the Latin neuter, which means neither of the two.

teile.einleitung: The Matterhorn is probably the most famous mountain in Switzerland. With its pyramid shape it is known all over the world and is a symbol of the Swiss Alps. It stands in the canton of Valais on the border with Italy, directly above the village of Zermatt.
wichtigste: The Matterhorn is 4478 metres high, so about 4500 metres.
It stands in the canton of Valais on the border with Italy.
The village of Zermatt lies at the foot of the mountain.
The Matterhorn is shaped like a pyramid with four steep faces.
The first ascent was made in 1865 by a roped party led by Edward Whymper.
In Italian the mountain is called Monte Cervino.
Every year many climbers try to reach the summit.

abschnitte.text: The **Matterhorn** stands in the Valais Alps on the border between Switzerland and Italy. It is 4478 metres high. The mountain has four steep faces, which point almost exactly north, east, south and west. Between them run four ridges, which is why it looks like a **pyramid**. On the Italian side lies the resort of Breuil-Cervinia.

For a long time the Matterhorn was thought to be impossible to climb. On 14 July 1865 a roped party led by the Englishman **Edward Whymper** became the first to reach the summit, via the Hörnli Ridge. On the way down, however, a rope broke and four of the seven men fell to their deaths. Only three days later, mountain guides from the Italian side also reached the summit. The disaster made the Matterhorn world-famous.

The rock of the summit pyramid originally comes from the **African plate**. When the Alps were formed, it was pushed over European rock. That is why people sometimes say the summit of the Matterhorn is African. The mountain got its sharp shape from **glaciers** that gnawed at it from all sides during the ice ages.

At the foot of the Matterhorn lies **Zermatt**, one of the best-known holiday resorts in Switzerland. The village is car-free: you arrive by train and get around in small electric vehicles. From Zermatt the **Gornergrat Railway** runs up to over 3000 metres, from where you have a wonderful view of the Matterhorn. In winter you can ski all around the mountain, even into Italy.

Most climbers climb the Matterhorn via the **Hörnli Ridge** from the Swiss side. They first spend the night in the Hörnli Hut at about 3260 metres and set off in the middle of the night. The climb is difficult and dangerous, so many go with an experienced **mountain guide**. More than 500 people have died on the Matterhorn.

The Matterhorn is a **landmark** of Switzerland and appears on postcards, stamps and souvenirs. Many people believe that the shape of Toblerone chocolate was inspired by the Matterhorn. For photographers, sunrise is especially beautiful when the summit glows red. The mountain attracts visitors from all over the world every year.

begriffe.erklaerung: A narrow, sharp edge where two sides of a mountain meet.
A group of climbers who are tied together with a rope.
The first time that people reach the summit of a mountain.
A place where no ordinary petrol-engined cars are allowed to drive.

gewusst: An iron cross stands on the summit of the Matterhorn.
The north face of the Matterhorn is one of the three great north faces of the Alps.
The rope that broke on the way down in 1865 can be seen today in the Matterhorn Museum in Zermatt.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. A different language is spoken depending on the region, and many people speak several. This variety is an important part of Swiss identity.
wichtigste: The four national languages are German, French, Italian and Romansh.
German is the national language spoken by the most people.
Romansh is spoken mainly in the Grisons.
The Italian word “Grazie” means “Thank you”.
In German-speaking Switzerland people speak dialect in everyday life but usually write standard German.
Romansh has been a national language since 1938.
At school children learn at least one other national language.

abschnitte.text: According to the Federal Constitution, Switzerland has four **national languages**. German, French and Italian are also **official languages** of the Confederation, which means that laws and forms are available in these languages. Romansh is an official language when dealing with people who speak Romansh. About 62 per cent of the population mainly speak German, about 23 per cent French, about 8 per cent Italian and less than 1 per cent Romansh (as of about 2022).

In German-speaking Switzerland people speak **Swiss German** in everyday life, that is various dialects such as Bernese German, Zurich German or Basel German. Writing, on the other hand, is mostly in standard German, which in Switzerland is called Schriftdeutsch, written German. Swiss standard German has its own words such as Velo (bicycle), Trottoir (pavement) or Znüni (mid-morning snack). Also, in Switzerland people do not write the German sharp s but always ss.

In the **Romandie** in the west people speak French, for example in Geneva, Lausanne and Neuchâtel. Italian is spoken in Ticino and in some southern valleys of the Grisons, such as the Mesolcina and the Val Poschiavo. Anyone who says “Grazie” is saying thank you in Italian; in French it is “Merci”. Some cantons are bilingual, namely Bern, Fribourg and Valais.

**Romansh** is a Romance language that comes from the Latin of the Romans. It is spoken mainly in the Grisons, which is the only canton with three official languages. There are five regional written forms, the idioms, for example Sursilvan and Vallader. Since 1982 there has also been the common written language Rumantsch Grischun. “Allegra” is a Romansh greeting.

Many people in Switzerland speak other languages as well as their mother tongue. Because of immigration, English, Portuguese, Albanian and many other languages are also spoken. On packaging and banknotes, texts are often in several national languages. The language border between German and French is jokingly called the **Röstigraben**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A language that is recognised in the constitution as a language of the country.
A language in which the authorities, laws and courts work.
The spoken language of a region.
One of the regional written forms of Romansh.

gewusst: Biel/Bienne is the largest bilingual town in Switzerland; many people there switch language in the middle of a conversation.
The word “merci” is not only used in the Romandie but also often in German-speaking Switzerland.
Less than one per cent of the population speak Romansh as their main language, yet it is still a national language.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is a small country without large raw materials, but it is one of the richest countries in the world. Its success rests on well-trained people, inventiveness, stable politics and strong industries such as pharmaceuticals, mechanical engineering, watches and banking.
wichtigste: Most working people in Switzerland work in the tertiary sector, that is in services.
Chemicals and pharmaceuticals make up the largest share of Swiss goods exports.
More than 99 per cent of companies are SMEs with fewer than 250 employees.
The Peace Agreement of 1937 is seen as the foundation of the Swiss social partnership.
The standard rate of VAT is 8.1 per cent (as of 2026).
The debt brake obliges the Confederation not to spend more than it takes in over an economic cycle.
The Competition Commission COMCO watches over cartels and company mergers.

abschnitte.text: Experts divide the economy into three sectors. The **primary sector** covers farming and forestry; in Switzerland only a few per cent of people still work there. The **secondary sector** is industry, that is factories, building and crafts. The **tertiary sector** covers services such as trade, banks, insurance, schools, hospitals and tourism. Today about three quarters of all working people work in this services sector.

The most important export industry is **chemicals and pharmaceuticals**, with companies such as Roche and Novartis in Basel. Switzerland is also known for its **watch industry** in the Jura and for machines, electrical engineering and metals, the MEM industry for short. Nestlé in Vevey is one of the largest food companies in the world. In addition there is the financial centre with banks and insurance companies, and tourism in the mountains and cities.

In 1937 employers and trade unions in the metal and machine industry concluded the **Peace Agreement**. They promised to settle disputes through negotiations rather than strikes. From this grew the social partnership, in which employers and employees together set wages and working conditions in **collective labour agreements**. That is why Switzerland has very few strikes compared with other countries.

The state is funded mainly through taxes, for example **VAT** of 8.1 per cent on most goods and services. A lower rate applies to food and books. The **debt brake** was accepted by a large majority of the people in 2001 and has applied since 2003. It is meant to stop the Confederation from running up more and more debt.

So that companies compete fairly with each other, there is the **Competition Commission COMCO**. It bans agreements on prices, so-called cartels, and examines large company mergers. More than 99 per cent of all Swiss firms are **SMEs**, small and medium-sized enterprises such as bakeries, joiners’ workshops or IT firms. Together they provide about two thirds of all jobs.

Switzerland earns a large part of its wealth from **exports**, that is sales abroad. Its most important trading partners are the countries of the European Union, the USA and China. Switzerland is linked with the EU through the **bilateral agreements**. Because Switzerland has no sea and hardly any raw materials, knowledge, quality and innovation are especially important.

begriffe.erklaerung: Selling goods and services abroad.
Small and medium-sized enterprises with fewer than 250 employees.
Employers and trade unions who negotiate wages and working conditions together.
A forbidden agreement between firms, for example about prices.
A rule that forces the Confederation not to spend more than it takes in over the long term.

gewusst: Switzerland has been in first place in the United Nations’ Global Innovation Index for many years.
Switzerland has no oil or ore deposits of its own and has to import almost all its raw materials.
The dual apprenticeship system, in which young people learn at a company and at school, is seen as a model all over the world.

teile.einleitung: The Rhine is one of the largest and most important rivers in Europe. It rises in the Swiss Alps and flows for about 1200 kilometres to the North Sea. On the way it plunges down at the Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen.
wichtigste: The Rhine is about 1200 kilometres long.
It is formed in the Grisons from the Vorderrhein and the Hinterrhein.
The Rhine flows through Lake Constance and on to Basel.
The Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen is the most famous waterfall in Switzerland.
Part of the border between Switzerland and Germany is formed by the Rhine.
In the Netherlands the Rhine flows into the North Sea.
Via the Rhine, Switzerland is connected with the sea by ship.

abschnitte.text: The Rhine has two headwaters. The **Vorderrhein** begins at Lake Toma near the Oberalp Pass. The **Hinterrhein** comes from the area of the Rheinwaldhorn. At Reichenau near Chur the two flow together and form the Alpine Rhine. This flows north and forms the border with Liechtenstein and Austria.

The Alpine Rhine flows into **Lake Constance**. At Stein am Rhein the river leaves the lake and is now called the **High Rhine**. It flows west to Basel and over long stretches forms the border between Switzerland and Germany. On the way it takes in the Aare, the longest river that runs entirely within Switzerland.

At Neuhausen am Rheinfall near Schaffhausen the water plunges over a rock step. The **Rhine Falls** is about 150 metres wide and around 23 metres high. Measured by the amount of water, it is one of the largest waterfalls in Europe. You can go by boat to a rock in the middle of the roaring water.

From Basel the Rhine can be navigated by large cargo ships. In the **Rhine ports** of Basel, crude oil, grain and containers are transferred. So although Switzerland has no access to the sea, it has a connection via the Rhine all the way to the port of Rotterdam. Many hydroelectric power stations on the Rhine also produce electricity.

The Rhine touches Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Austria, Germany, France and the Netherlands. After Basel it flows through the **Upper Rhine Plain** and then north past cities such as Cologne. In the Netherlands it splits into several branches and flows into the **North Sea**. Because it is so important for trade and transport, it is sometimes called the lifeline of Europe.

In Basel, **swimming in the Rhine** is very popular in summer. You pack your clothes into a waterproof bag, the Wickelfisch, and let the current carry you. Basel also has ferries that are pulled across the river only by the current. When swimming, though, you must watch out carefully for ships and strong currents.

begriffe.erklaerung: A river that, together with others, forms a larger river.
The place where a river flows into a sea, a lake or another river.
The section of the Rhine between Lake Constance and Basel.
A port on the Rhine where cargo ships are loaded and unloaded.

gewusst: A drop of water from the Alps of the Grisons takes several days to reach the North Sea.
Where it joins the Rhine, the Aare often carries more water than the Rhine itself.
On summer days the Rhine Falls is so loud that you can hear it roaring from far away.

teile.einleitung: A Räbeliechtli is a lantern made from a hollowed-out turnip, called a Räbe. In late autumn children in German-speaking Switzerland carve patterns into them and carry the glowing turnips through the dark streets in a procession.
wichtigste: A Räbe is a white turnip, also called an autumn turnip.
It is hollowed out and patterns are carved into the skin.
A candle burns inside and makes the patterns glow.
The Räbeliechtli procession usually takes place in November.
During it people sing the song “Räbeliechtli, wo gosch hii?” (Little turnip light, where are you going?).
The largest procession is the Räbechilbi in Richterswil.

abschnitte.text: The **Räbe** is a white **turnip** that is harvested in autumn. It is also called an **autumn turnip** or table turnip. In the past it was an important vegetable for the winter and was also fed to animals. It has a firm skin and white flesh. That is why it is good for carving.

First you cut a lid off the top and hollow out the turnip with a spoon. Then you scratch **patterns** into the skin, for example stars, moons or flowers. You do not cut right through but only remove the outer skin. A **candle** or a tea light goes inside. When it burns, the patterns shimmer warmly through the turnip.

In **November**, when it gets dark early, many municipalities hold a **Räbeliechtli procession**. The children carry their turnip on a string through the streets. The street lamps are often switched off for it. They sing songs such as **“Räbeliechtli, wo gosch hii?”**. Nursery schools and schools often organise the procession together with the parents.

The best-known procession is the **Räbechilbi** in **Richterswil** on Lake Zurich. Many tonnes of turnips are carved there. It is not only children who carry lanterns: houses and floats are also decorated with turnips. It is considered the largest turnip lantern procession in the world. Many visitors travel there for it.

gewusst: The custom recalls autumn festivals that people used to hold to celebrate the end of the harvest.
At the Räbechilbi in Richterswil, whole houses are lit up with patterns made of turnips.

teile.einleitung: Swiss companies make food, medicines, watches and machines that are sold all over the world. As well as some very large corporations, there are hundreds of thousands of small and medium-sized businesses. Together they help make Switzerland one of the wealthiest countries in the world.
wichtigste: The food company Nestlé has its headquarters in Vevey.
Gottlieb Duttweiler founded Migros in 1925.
SBB stands for Swiss Federal Railways.
The pharmaceutical companies Roche and Novartis have their headquarters in Basel.
In the Jura arc from Geneva to Schaffhausen, the watch industry is especially important.
More than 99 per cent of Swiss companies are small and medium-sized enterprises.
Many Swiss firms sell most of their products abroad.

abschnitte.text: **Nestlé** was founded in 1866 in Vevey on Lake Geneva, where Henri Nestlé developed a powdered milk for babies. Today Nestlé is the largest food company in the world. It owns brands for coffee, chocolate, water and pet food. Chocolate makers such as Lindt & Sprüngli from Kilchberg are also world-famous.

Gottlieb Duttweiler founded **Migros** in Zurich in 1925. At first five sales vans drove through the neighbourhoods offering goods more cheaply than the shops. In 1941 Duttweiler turned Migros into a **cooperative** that belongs to its members. Its biggest competitor is Coop; the two are the largest retailers in Switzerland.

The **Swiss Federal Railways** (SBB) were created in 1902 and belong to the Confederation. They run one of the densest rail networks in the world and carry hundreds of thousands of people every day. Swiss Post and Swisscom also belong wholly or mainly to the Confederation. Such companies are called federally owned companies.

The pharmaceutical companies **Roche** and **Novartis** have their headquarters in **Basel**. Roche was founded in 1896, and Novartis was created in 1996 from the merger of Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz. They develop medicines and diagnostic tests that are used in almost every country. The pharmaceutical industry is now Switzerland’s most important export sector.

The **watch industry** is at home in the **Jura arc**, from Geneva via Biel to Schaffhausen. Well-known brands are Rolex from Geneva and the Swatch Group based in Biel, whose colourful Swatch watch came onto the market in 1983. Every year Switzerland exports watches worth many billions of francs. Machines, precision instruments and Victorinox pocket knives are also in demand.

Switzerland is also known for its banks and insurance companies; the largest bank is UBS, based in Zurich. In 2023 it took over Credit Suisse. But most of the economy is made up of **SMEs**, small and medium-sized enterprises with fewer than 250 employees. These include bakeries, joiners’ workshops, engineering offices and many other businesses.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large company, often with many subsidiaries in several countries.
The place where a company is managed from.
A company that belongs jointly to its members.
Small and medium-sized enterprises with fewer than 250 employees.
Selling goods abroad.

gewusst: As a matter of principle, Migros does not sell alcohol or cigarettes in its supermarkets.
Migros started in 1925 with only five lorries that went round as mobile shops.
Nestlé still has its headquarters in Vevey, where the company was founded more than 150 years ago.

teile.einleitung: Many cows in Switzerland wear a bell around their neck on the pasture or the alp. The ringing shows the farmer where the animals are. But cowbells are also part of tradition and a popular souvenir.
wichtigste: The bell rings when the cow moves.
This lets the farmer hear where the cows are on the pasture.
There are cast bells and forged Treicheln.
When the cows go up to the alp, they often wear especially large, decorated bells.
Cowbells are also popular presents and prizes, for example at Swiss wrestling festivals.

abschnitte.text: On large pastures and **alps** it is not always easy to see all the cows. They quickly disappear behind hills, in the woods or in the fog. The **bell** rings with every movement. This lets the farmer or the alp herdswoman hear where the herd is. A trained ear can even recognise individual cows by the sound of their bell.

There are two kinds. The **bell** is **cast** from metal such as bronze or brass and has a bright sound. The **Treichel** is **forged** from sheet metal and has a duller, deeper tone. Treicheln can be very large and heavy. Both are held on a broad **leather strap**, which is often beautifully embroidered.

In early summer the farmers take their cattle up to the alp; this is called the **Alpaufzug**. In autumn they come back down, at the **Alpabzug**. On these days the cows often wear their most beautiful and largest bells. The animals are decorated with flowers and garlands. Many people come to see and hear the procession.

Cowbells are a sign of **Swiss mountain culture**. At **Swiss wrestling festivals**, winners often receive a large bell as a prize. In some customs people carry Treicheln and walk through the village ringing them, for example at the **Trychlen**. Many tourists buy small bells as **souvenirs**. In some villages there are also arguments because the ringing at night disturbs local residents.

gewusst: Large Treicheln can be so heavy that cows only wear them on special occasions.
Some farming families collect bells over generations and are proud of their special sound.

teile.einleitung: In some votes in Switzerland, it is not only how many people say yes that counts. The cantons also have a vote, the cantonal vote. Six cantons have only half a vote.
wichtigste: In votes each canton has one cantonal vote; six cantons have half a vote.
These six are Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden.
They used to be called half-cantons.
Together there are 23 cantonal votes.
The majority of the cantonal votes is called the majority of the cantons.
Changes to the constitution need a popular majority and a majority of the cantons.

abschnitte.text: A canton is also called a **Stand**. That is why its vote in a ballot is called a **Standesstimme**, a cantonal vote. The result in the canton decides how this vote counts. If a majority in the canton says yes, the cantonal vote counts as yes. Switzerland has 26 cantons. Twenty of them have a whole vote and six have half a vote.

Obwalden and Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft, and Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden each have **half a cantonal vote**. These cantons were created by dividing a former territory. That is why they were called **half-cantons**. Today the Federal Constitution speaks of cantons with half a cantonal vote. In the Council of States they each have one seat instead of two.

A change to the **Federal Constitution** needs two majorities. First, the **popular majority**: more than half of those voting say yes. Second, the **majority of the cantons**: the majority of the 23 cantonal votes say yes. If it is 11.5 to 11.5, the majority of the cantons has not been reached. This is meant to stop small cantons from simply being outvoted by the large ones.

In 2020 slightly more than half of the voters said yes to the **Responsible Business Initiative**. But the majority of the cantons said no. That is why the initiative was rejected. Such cases are rare, but they show how important the cantonal votes are. Whether this system is a good one is debated again and again.

gewusst: For the majority of the cantons, a voter in the smallest canton has much more weight than a voter in the canton of Zurich.
Canton names such as “Obwalden and Nidwalden” are still a reminder today that they once belonged together.

teile.einleitung: The Schwägalp is a pass and an alpine pasture area at the foot of the Säntis in eastern Switzerland. From here the cable car runs up the highest mountain of the Alpstein.
wichtigste: The Schwägalp lies in the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden.
The valley station of the Säntis cable car is on the Schwägalp.
At 2502 metres, the Säntis is the highest mountain in the Alpstein.
A pass road runs over the Schwägalp between the Appenzell region and the Toggenburg.
In summer cows graze here, and in winter cross-country skiers and snowshoers come.

abschnitte.titel: By cable car up the Säntis
abschnitte.text: The **Säntis cable car** is an aerial cableway. Its valley station stands on the Schwägalp. In a few minutes the cabin glides almost to the summit of the **Säntis**. At the top, in good weather, you have a wide view. You can see as far as Lake Constance and into several countries. On the summit there is also a weather station and a tall transmitter tower.

The **Alpstein** is a limestone mountain range in eastern Switzerland. It lies in the cantons of Appenzell Innerrhoden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and St Gallen. Its highest peak is the Säntis. In the Alpstein there are many hiking trails, mountain lakes and mountain inns. The Schwägalp lies on the north side of the Säntis.

An **alp** is a mountain pasture where the cows graze in summer. Cows spend the warm months on the Schwägalp too. Cheese is made from the milk. On the Schwägalp there is a **show dairy**, where visitors can watch how cheese is made. A Swiss wrestling festival also takes place here regularly, the **Schwägalp-Schwinget**.

gewusst: In clear weather you can see six countries from the Säntis: Switzerland, Germany, Austria, Liechtenstein, France and Italy.

teile.einleitung: Rösti is one of the best-known dishes in Switzerland. It is made from grated potatoes that are fried in the pan until golden brown and crispy. It originally comes from the canton of Bern.
wichtigste: Rösti is made from grated potatoes.
It is fried in butter or fat in the pan.
On the outside it is golden brown and crispy, on the inside soft.
Raw or boiled potatoes are used.
Rösti used to be a farmers’ breakfast in the canton of Bern.
The “Röstigraben” is named after it.

abschnitte.text: For a rösti you grate **potatoes** with a coarse grater. Some people use **raw** potatoes, others potatoes boiled in their skins the day before, called **Gschwellti**. The grated potatoes go into a hot pan with **butter** or fat and are pressed flat. After a while you turn the rösti over, often with the help of a plate. When both sides are **golden brown**, it is ready.

In the past, farmers in the **canton of Bern** often ate rösti in the morning. It gave them lots of strength for the hard work in the fields. With it they drank milk or milky coffee. Over time rösti became popular throughout **German-speaking Switzerland**. Today it is eaten mainly for lunch or dinner.

Rösti can be made in many different ways. For **Bernese rösti**, bacon is fried with it. Others put onions, cheese or a **fried egg** on top. Rösti is very well known as a side dish with **Zürcher Geschnetzeltes**, Zurich-style sliced veal. In restaurants you are often served a large, round rösti straight in the pan.

The **Röstigraben**, the “rösti ditch”, is named after rösti. This is the joking name for the language border between **German-speaking Switzerland** and the **Romandie**. The name comes from the fact that rösti used to be eaten mainly in German-speaking Switzerland. When the two parts of the country decide differently in a vote, people often talk about the Röstigraben. In French it is also called the “Rideau de rösti”, the rösti curtain.

gewusst: Abroad, rösti is often seen as a typical Swiss national dish.
Many rösti fans love to argue about whether to use raw or boiled potatoes.

teile.einleitung: Magenbrot is a sweet, brown pastry in small pieces. It is coated with a shiny glaze and tastes of spices. In Switzerland people often buy it at markets and at the funfair.
wichtigste: Magenbrot is made of small pieces of gingerbread dough.
It has a shiny, sweet glaze, often with cocoa.
Typical spices are cinnamon, cloves and aniseed.
People like to buy it in a little paper bag.
It belongs to markets, funfairs and the Christmas season.

abschnitte.text: Magenbrot is a pastry made from a dough similar to **gingerbread**. It contains **honey** or sugar, flour and lots of **spices** such as cinnamon, cloves and aniseed. The dough is shaped into bars, baked and cut into small pieces. Then the pieces are given a **glaze** of sugar and often **cocoa**. They then shine brown and are slightly crunchy outside and soft inside.

abschnitte.titel: At the market and the funfair
abschnitte.text: Magenbrot is a typical **market treat**. At the **Chilbi** funfair, at autumn fairs and at **Christmas markets**, stalls sell it in small paper bags. The smell of cinnamon and sugar attracts many people. You can also buy it in shops, especially in autumn and winter. Magenbrot is also known in Germany and Austria.

The name **Magenbrot** means “stomach bread” and sounds as if it has something to do with the stomach. In the past people believed the spices in it were good for **digestion**. That is why people liked to eat it after a big meal. But it is not really bread. Today people simply eat it because it tastes good.

gewusst: Many of the spices in Magenbrot, such as cinnamon and cloves, used to come from far away and were very expensive.
You can also bake Magenbrot yourself, but it takes a bit of patience.

teile.einleitung: Each of the 26 cantons has a capital. The cantonal government and usually also the cantonal parliament have their seat there. The capital is not always the largest town in the canton.
wichtigste: The cantonal capital is the seat of a canton’s government.
The capital of Ticino is Bellinzona, not the larger Lugano.
The capital of the Valais is Sion, in German Sitten.
The capital of the canton of Jura is Delémont, in German Delsberg.
In Appenzell Ausserrhoden the government and parliament sit in Herisau.
The capital of Nidwalden is Stans.
Bern is both the capital of the canton of Bern and the federal city of Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: A **capital** is the town or village from which a canton is governed. The **cantonal government** meets here; depending on the canton it is called the Regierungsrat or the Conseil d’État. Usually the cantonal parliament also meets there, such as the Kantonsrat or the Grosser Rat. The most important courts and offices of the canton are often in the capital too. Many capitals have the same name as their canton, for example Zurich, Lucerne or Glarus.

abschnitte.titel: Capitals in the south and west
abschnitte.text: **Bellinzona** is the capital of Ticino and is famous for its three castles, which are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The largest town in Ticino, however, is Lugano. In the Valais, **Sion** is the capital; the castles of Valère and Tourbillon tower above the town. The capital of the canton of Jura is Delémont. In the Romandie there are other capitals such as Lausanne in Vaud, Fribourg and Neuchâtel.

In Central Switzerland the capitals are often small places. **Stans** is the capital of Nidwalden, Sarnen of Obwalden, Altdorf of Uri, and Schwyz of the canton of the same name. The famous Tell monument stands in Altdorf. In Schwyz the Federal Charter of 1291 is kept in the Museum of the Swiss Charters of Confederation.

In the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden the constitution does not name an official capital. The government and parliament sit in **Herisau**, but the high court is in Trogen. The canton of Bern has in the city of Bern a capital that is also the **federal city**. Officially Switzerland has no capital city; Bern is only described as the seat of the federal authorities.

In the east of Switzerland, Chur in the Grisons, **St Gallen**, Frauenfeld in Thurgau, Herisau and Appenzell are important capitals. In the north lie Schaffhausen, Aarau in Aargau, Liestal in Basel-Landschaft, and Basel. On the Swiss Plateau there are also Solothurn, Zug and Zurich. Chur is considered one of the oldest towns in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: The place from which a canton is governed.
The government of a canton in many German-speaking cantons.
What Bern is called, because the Federal Council and parliament have their seat there.
The French-speaking part of Switzerland.

gewusst: With only about 6000 inhabitants, Appenzell is one of the smallest cantonal capitals.
The castles of Bellinzona have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000.
Sion lies in the Rhône valley and is one of the sunniest places in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Easter is the most important festival in Christianity. It recalls the resurrection of Jesus. In Switzerland colourful eggs, the Easter Bunny and egg tapping are also part of it.
wichtigste: At Easter Christians celebrate the resurrection of Jesus.
Easter always falls on a Sunday in March or April.
Good Friday and Easter Monday are public holidays in most cantons.
People dye eggs and hide them for the children.
In egg tapping (Eiertütschen) two boiled eggs are knocked together.
Whoever’s egg stays whole wins.

abschnitte.text: According to the **Bible**, Jesus was crucified on a Friday and rose from the dead on the third day. **Good Friday** and **Easter Sunday** recall this. That is why Easter is the most important festival of the year for Christians. Before Easter comes **Lent**, which begins on Ash Wednesday. The week before Easter is called **Holy Week**.

abschnitte.titel: A festival without a fixed date
abschnitte.text: Easter has a different date every year. It is the **first Sunday after the first full moon in spring**. That is why Easter always falls between 22 March and 25 April. Other holidays such as **Ascension Day** and **Whitsun** also depend on the date of Easter. In most cantons Good Friday and **Easter Monday** are days off.

The **egg** is a sign of new life. Before Easter many families dye boiled eggs in bright colours. On Easter morning the children look for the eggs and chocolate bunnies that the **Easter Bunny** has hidden. **Osterfladen**, an Easter tart with semolina or rice, is often part of it too. Many shops sell chocolate bunnies in all sizes.

A popular game is **egg tapping**, called Eiertütschen. Two people each hold a boiled egg and knock the **tips** together. One egg gets a crack. Whoever’s egg **stays whole** wins and may play on. In Zurich there is also **Zwänzgerle**: adults try to throw a 20-centime coin into an egg that a child is holding.

gewusst: Easter can be no earlier than 22 March and no later than 25 April.
Easter eggs are often dyed with onion skins, which give the eggs a reddish-brown colour.

teile.einleitung: Fasnacht is a colourful festival in late winter. Young and old dress up, and there are parades, loud music and lots of confetti. In Switzerland it is especially popular in Basel, Lucerne and many villages.
wichtigste: At Fasnacht many people dress up in costumes and masks.
It takes place before Lent, which begins before Easter.
Parades, Guggenmusik bands and confetti are typical.
In many places Dirty Thursday is the start.
The Basel Fasnacht begins with the Morgestraich at 4 o’clock in the morning.
The noise is meant to drive away winter symbolically.

abschnitte.text: The word **Fasnacht** is connected with **Lent** (in German “Fastenzeit”, the time of fasting). Christians traditionally fast for about 40 days before Easter. Before this quiet time begins, people celebrate wildly one last time. That is why Fasnacht falls in **February or March**, depending on when Easter is. In Protestant areas it is often celebrated a little later, as in **Basel**.

At Fasnacht many people slip into a different role. Children dress up as animals, pirates, princesses or characters from films. Adults often wear elaborate masks; in Basel they are called **Larven**. Many belong to a **Clique** or a **Guggenmusik** band and share a costume, which they often spend months making themselves.

**Guggenmusik** bands are typical of Swiss Fasnacht. They deliberately play a little out of tune on trumpets, trombones and big drums. In Basel, groups with **piccolos** and **drums** also march through the narrow streets. Decorated floats take part in the parades and it rains **confetti**, which in Basel is called **Räppli**. The noise is meant to drive away **winter**.

The **Basel Fasnacht** begins on the Monday after Ash Wednesday with the **Morgestraich** at 4 o’clock in the morning. Then all the lights in the city centre go out and only the lanterns shine. The **Lucerne Fasnacht** starts early in the morning on Dirty Thursday with a loud bang. Many other places also have their own customs, such as the **Chesslete** in Solothurn.

gewusst: The Basel Fasnacht has been on the UNESCO list of intangible cultural heritage since 2017.
The Basel Fasnacht lasts exactly three days, which are also called “die drey scheenschte Dääg”, the three most beautiful days.

teile.einleitung: The Grittibänz is a little man made of sweet plaited bread dough. In Switzerland people eat it around St Nicholas Day on 6 December. It often has raisin eyes and decorations made of dough.
wichtigste: The Grittibänz is a figure made of sweet yeast dough.
It is eaten mainly around 6 December, St Nicholas Day.
The eyes and buttons are often made of raisins.
In Basel it is called Grättimaa.
Many families bake it themselves.

abschnitte.text: The Grittibänz is baked from **Zopf dough**, the dough of Swiss plaited bread, or a similar sweet **yeast dough**. You shape a head, a body, arms and legs. **Raisins** are used for the eyes and buttons, and sometimes almonds or pearl sugar too. Before baking it is brushed with egg so that it shines nicely. Many children bake it at school or at home.

The Grittibänz belongs to **St Nicholas Day** on **6 December**. On this day the Samichlaus, the Swiss St Nicholas, visits the children with his companion, the **Schmutzli**. He brings nuts, mandarins, gingerbread and chocolate. The Grittibänz is often in the St Nicholas sack too. Bakeries sell it from the end of November.

The name has two parts. **Gritti** has to do with “grittig”, which means with legs apart. **Bänz** is an old short form of the name **Benedikt** and used to be a common man’s name. In **Basel** people say **Grättimaa**, and in other areas there are other names. It always means the same little dough man.

gewusst: Some Grittibänzen hold a small clay pipe in their hand.
Similar dough figures also exist in Germany, where they are called Weckmann, for example.

teile.einleitung: The right to vote is the right to take part in votes and elections. In Switzerland, Swiss citizens aged 18 and over may have their say at federal level, and they do so several times a year.
wichtigste: At federal level you may vote and take part in elections from the age of 18.
For this you must have Swiss citizenship.
Women only received the right to vote at federal level in 1971.
In the canton of Glarus people have been allowed to vote on cantonal matters from 16 since 2007.
Swiss citizens living abroad may also take part in federal votes.
Votes usually take place on four Sundays a year.

abschnitte.text: In **federal** votes and elections, all Swiss citizens who are **18 years** old may take part. This also applies to people who live abroad. People speak of the **right to vote** when you may vote, and of the **right to stand for election** when you can be elected yourself. The papers come to your home by post. Many people vote by post; others go to the polling station on Sunday.

In cantons and municipalities, some rules are different. In the canton of **Glarus**, young people have been allowed to vote on cantonal and municipal matters from the age of 16 since 2007. Some cantons, for example Neuchâtel and Jura, also give **foreign residents** the right to vote at municipal level. The voters of the cantons decide on such rules themselves.

For a long time only men were allowed to vote. At federal level women only received the **right to vote** in **1971**. That made Switzerland one of the last countries in Europe. The canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden only introduced women’s suffrage at cantonal level in 1990, after a ruling by the **Federal Supreme Court**.

abschnitte.titel: Having a say through initiatives and referendums
abschnitte.text: People who have the right to vote can also start something themselves. With a **popular initiative** you can demand a change to the Federal Constitution. This requires 100,000 signatures in 18 months. With a **referendum** you can demand a vote on a new law. This requires 50,000 signatures in 100 days. This form is called **direct democracy**.

gewusst: Switzerland holds votes more often than almost any other country in the world.
In Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden people vote by raising their hand in the open air at the Landsgemeinde.

teile.einleitung: Hardly any country is home to as many international organisations as Switzerland. Geneva in particular is a meeting place for the world, but Basel, Bern and Lausanne are also the seats of important organisations. People from almost every country work together here on issues such as peace, health, trade and sport.
wichtigste: Geneva is the European seat of the UN and home to many organisations.
The International Committee of the Red Cross was founded in Geneva in 1863.
The League of Nations had its seat in Geneva from 1920 to 1946.
The World Trade Organization WTO in Geneva regulates world trade.
CERN near Geneva runs the largest particle accelerator in the world.
The Bank for International Settlements has its seat in Basel.
The Universal Postal Union is based in Bern, the International Olympic Committee in Lausanne.

abschnitte.text: An **international organisation** is a group of several states that pursue a goal together. Examples are the UN, which works for peace, or the World Health Organization **WHO**. There are also non-governmental organisations, **NGOs** for short, which were not founded by states. Sports federations such as FIFA in Zurich or UEFA in Nyon also belong to this group. Because of its neutrality, Switzerland is seen as an ideal host.

abschnitte.titel: Geneva as a world meeting place
abschnitte.text: In 1863 Henry Dunant and other people from Geneva founded the **International Committee of the Red Cross** (ICRC). From 1920 to 1946 the **League of Nations**, the forerunner of the UN, had its seat in Geneva. Today the European headquarters of the UN is there in the Palais des Nations. The WHO, the UN Refugee Agency UNHCR, the International Labour Organization and the World Trade Organization **WTO** also have their seats in Geneva. That is why thousands of diplomats live in the city.

**CERN** is the European Organization for Nuclear Research and was founded in 1954. Its site lies near Meyrin on the border between Switzerland and France. There it runs the **Large Hadron Collider**, a particle accelerator in a tunnel around 27 kilometres long. Researchers there study the smallest building blocks of matter. The World Wide Web was also invented at CERN around 1990.

The **Bank for International Settlements** (BIS), the bank of the central banks, founded in 1930, is based in Basel. Bern is the seat of the **Universal Postal Union**, which was founded in 1874 and is now a specialised agency of the UN. The **International Olympic Committee** has had its seat in Lausanne since 1915. That is why Lausanne calls itself the Olympic capital.

Although the UN seat in Geneva had existed for a long time, Switzerland only joined the **UN** in 2002. The people had clearly rejected joining in 1986 and voted in favour in 2002. Switzerland supports international organisations with buildings, loans and tax advantages. In return they bring jobs and prestige to the country. In 2023 and 2024 Switzerland was even a member of the **UN Security Council**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The United Nations, an organisation of almost every state in the world for peace and cooperation.
An organisation that was not founded by a state, for example an aid organisation.
A person who represents their country to other states or organisations.
A machine that makes tiny particles go very fast and collide.

gewusst: Henry Dunant received the very first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.
The world’s first website went online at CERN in 1991.
The ICRC has received the Nobel Peace Prize three times.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is a land of mountains. More than half of its area belongs to the Alps, and in the north-west the Jura mountains rise as well. The highest peak in Switzerland is the Dufourspitze in the Monte Rosa massif.
wichtigste: Switzerland has three large landscapes: the Alps, the Swiss Plateau and the Jura.
The Alps cover around 60 per cent of the country’s area.
The highest mountain is the Dufourspitze in the Monte Rosa massif, at 4634 metres.
The Jura lies in the north-west along the border with France.
The Gotthard Pass links the canton of Uri with Ticino.
The Great Aletsch Glacier is the largest glacier in the Alps.
The Alps were formed by the collision of the African and the Eurasian plates.

abschnitte.text: The **Alps** stretch in a great arc through the centre and south of Switzerland. Here there are many **four-thousanders**, mountains over 4000 metres high, such as the Matterhorn, the Dom or the Finsteraarhorn. The highest peak is the Dufourspitze in the Monte Rosa massif on the border with Italy. Other well-known areas are the Bernese Oberland with the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau, and the Engadine in the Grisons.

The **Jura** is a range of lower mountains in the north-west of Switzerland along the border with France. It is made mainly of **limestone**, which was laid down in a sea millions of years ago. That is why fossils are often found there. The highest Swiss summit in the Jura is Mont Tendre in the canton of Vaud, at 1679 metres. The Jura mountains even gave their name to a geological period, the Jurassic, the time of the dinosaurs.

The Alps formed because the **African plate** pushed against Europe. Over many millions of years, layers of rock were folded up and pushed on top of each other. Later the Jura was also pressed into folds by this pressure. Glaciers in the ice ages then carved the valleys out deeply. This created the typical U-shaped valleys and many lakes.

Many **passes** lead over the Alps, for example the Gotthard Pass, the San Bernardino Pass and the Simplon Pass. The Gotthard Pass, at 2106 metres, links Uri with Ticino. Beneath it runs the **Gotthard Base Tunnel**, which opened in 2016 and, at 57 kilometres, is the longest railway tunnel in the world. In winter many pass roads are closed because of snow.

There are many **glaciers** in the Swiss Alps; the largest is the Great Aletsch Glacier in the Valais. Because of climate change the glaciers are melting fast and getting smaller every year. The mountains are also important for tourism, with skiing, hiking and mountaineering. Animals such as ibex, chamois, marmots and bearded vultures live in the Alps.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mountain that is more than 4000 metres high.
A way across a mountain range, usually at the lowest point between two mountains.
A huge mass of ice that moves slowly down the valley.
A group of mountains that belong closely together.

gewusst: The Dufourspitze was named after General Guillaume-Henri Dufour, who had the first accurate map of Switzerland made.
Fossilised dinosaur footprints have been found in the Jura.
The Great Aletsch Glacier is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch.

teile.einleitung: Swiss National Day is the national holiday of Switzerland and is celebrated every year on 1 August. It recalls the alliance of the three forest cantons in 1291, with which the history of the Confederation traditionally begins. On this day there are bonfires, paper lanterns, speeches and fireworks all over the country.
wichtigste: National Day takes place every year on 1 August.
It recalls the year 1291 and the Federal Charter of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden.
The Rütli Oath is said to have taken place on the Rütli meadow on Lake Uri.
In the evening, bonfires are lit on hills and mountains.
In the evening children often carry paper lanterns through the streets.
The day was first celebrated in 1891.
Since 1994, 1 August has been a public holiday off work throughout Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: 1 August recalls the **Federal Charter** of 1291, in which Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden promised each other help at the beginning of August. This alliance is seen as the founding document of the Confederation. Today the Federal Charter is on display in the Museum of the Swiss Charters of Confederation in Schwyz. Historians do not know every detail of exactly how the founding happened.

abschnitte.titel: The Rütli and the Rütli Oath
abschnitte.text: According to legend, representatives of the three valley communities met on the **Rütli**, a meadow on the shore of Lake Uri. There they are said to have sworn the **Rütli Oath** and promised each other eternal loyalty. This story was later linked with the legend of William Tell. Today the Rütli belongs to the Confederation, and a celebration takes place there every year.

For a long time Switzerland had no common national holiday. For the 600th anniversary, 1 August was celebrated nationwide for the first time in **1891**. From then on the day was marked every year, but in many places it was a normal working day. Only after a popular vote in 1993 did it become a public holiday off work throughout Switzerland from 1994.

In the evening large **bonfires** burn on hills and mountains and can be seen from far around. Children walk through the streets with colourful **paper lanterns**, and in many places there are fireworks. In the municipalities politicians give speeches, and the President of the Confederation addresses the population with a speech. Houses and streets are decorated with Swiss and cantonal flags.

The **1 August brunch** on many farms is very popular; people eat Zopf, plaited bread, with cheese and butter from the farm. Bakeries sell the 1 August roll, a bread roll with a small Swiss flag. Big firework displays take place, for example, at the Rhine Falls, which is then lit up in colour. Because of dry weather, fires and fireworks are banned in some years and regions.

begriffe.erklaerung: The document of 1291 in which Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden promised each other help.
A meadow on Lake Uri where the Rütli Oath is said to have taken place.
A large fire that is lit on a hill or mountain.
A lantern made of colourful paper with a candle or small lamp inside.

gewusst: 1 August only became a legal public holiday throughout Switzerland in 1994.
The original Federal Charter is written in Latin.
Before 1 August was chosen in 1891, Switzerland had no common national holiday.

teile.einleitung: The Rigi is a mountain massif in Central Switzerland between Lake Lucerne and Lake Zug. It is called the “Queen of the Mountains”. Since 1871 a cogwheel railway has run up to the summit, one of the first mountain railways in Europe.
wichtigste: The Rigi is called the “Queen of the Mountains”.
It lies between Lake Lucerne, Lake Zug and Lake Lauerz.
The highest point is called Rigi Kulm and is just under 1800 metres above sea level.
Since 1871 the cogwheel railway has run up from Vitznau.
It was the first mountain cogwheel railway in Europe.
The Rigi belongs to the cantons of Schwyz and Lucerne.

abschnitte.text: The **Rigi** is not especially high, but its **view** is famous. From the summit, **Rigi Kulm**, you can see far into the Alps and over many lakes in clear weather. That is why it is called the **Queen of the Mountains**. In German people say “die Rigi”, using the feminine form, because the mountain is feminine in Swiss German. The Rigi lies in the cantons of **Schwyz** and **Lucerne**.

In 1871 the **Vitznau-Rigi Railway** opened. It was the first **mountain cogwheel railway in Europe**. On a cogwheel railway, a toothed wheel under the train grips a toothed rack between the rails. This lets the train climb steep sections without slipping. A few years later the railway from **Arth-Goldau** was added.

As early as the 19th century, many people from all over Europe travelled up the Rigi. The **sunrise** on the summit was particularly popular. For this the guests spent the night in the hotels at the top and got up early. Famous writers and artists also visited the mountain. This made the Rigi one of the first places of **tourism** in the Alps.

Today you can reach the Rigi with two cogwheel railways and an **aerial cableway** from Weggis. In summer there are many **hiking trails**, and in winter sledging runs and ski slopes. There are hardly any cars on the Rigi; most visitors come by train. From the top you can see Lake Lucerne and **Lake Zug**, among other things. When there is fog in the valley, the summit is often in sunshine.

gewusst: The Rigi railway brought cogwheel technology to Switzerland, and many more cogwheel railways were built later.
The Rigi is almost completely surrounded by lakes.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is made up of 26 cantons. Each canton has its own constitution, its own parliament, its own government and its own courts. The cantons are very different, from huge mountain cantons to small city cantons.
wichtigste: Switzerland has 26 cantons.
The largest canton is the Grisons and the smallest is Basel-Stadt.
The name of Switzerland comes from the canton of Schwyz.
The Jura is the youngest canton and was created in 1979.
Six cantons used to be called half-cantons.
The canton of Zurich has the most inhabitants.
Each canton has a coat of arms and a two-letter code.

abschnitte.text: A **canton** is a member state of Switzerland, similar to a federal state in Germany. The cantons have a lot of power, for example over schools, police, health and taxes. Each canton has a **capital**, where the government and parliament have their seat. The cantons in turn are divided into municipalities. On car number plates and in addresses you often see the canton code, such as BE for Bern.

The largest canton is the **Grisons**, with over 7000 square kilometres, which is more than a sixth of Switzerland. The smallest is **Basel-Stadt**, with only around 37 square kilometres. The most people live in the canton of Zurich, about 1.6 million (as of 2024). Appenzell Innerrhoden has the fewest inhabitants, with about 16,000 people.

The first cantons were Uri, **Schwyz** and Unterwalden, which formed an alliance in 1291. The name Switzerland and the cross in the flag come from Schwyz. By 1513 the Confederation had grown to 13 members, including Lucerne, Zurich and Bern. In 1803 six new cantons such as Aargau, Thurgau and Ticino were added, and in 1815 Valais, Neuchâtel and Geneva. The youngest canton, the **Jura**, separated from the canton of Bern in 1979.

Some cantons used to be divided and were called **half-cantons**: Obwalden and Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft, and Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden. Today they are called cantons with half a cantonal vote. They each send only one person instead of two to the Council of States. In popular votes, their cantonal vote counts as half.

The cantons have different **official languages**. Most are German-speaking; Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel and Jura are French-speaking, and Ticino is Italian-speaking. Bern, Fribourg and Valais are bilingual, and the Grisons is even trilingual, with German, Romansh and Italian. Each canton has its own coat of arms, its own customs and often its own speciality in the kitchen.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the 26 member states of Switzerland.
Former name for a canton that has only half a cantonal vote.
Two letters that stand for a canton, for example ZH or GR.
The language in which the authorities and schools of a canton work.

gewusst: The canton of the Grisons is larger in area than the cantons of Bern and Valais, which come second and third.
The canton of Basel-Stadt consists of only three municipalities: Basel, Riehen and Bettingen.
Because of its many valleys, the Grisons is also called the land of 150 valleys.

teile.einleitung: Social insurance protects people in Switzerland from the financial consequences of old age, illness, accidents, disability and unemployment. Almost everyone has to take part and pay contributions. In this way the community helps those who get into a difficult situation.
wichtigste: The AVS was introduced in 1948.
The AVS is financed mainly on a pay-as-you-go basis.
Since 1972 the three-pillar principle of old-age provision has been written into the Federal Constitution.
The AVS contribution rate is 8.7 per cent of wages, not counting IV and EO (as of 2026).
The minimum conversion rate in occupational pensions is 6.8 per cent (as of 2026).
The lowest standard health insurance deductible for adults is 300 francs (as of 2026).
Pillar 3a belongs to the third pillar, private provision.

abschnitte.text: **Social insurance** is insurance that the state makes compulsory for everyone or almost everyone. The most important are old-age and survivors’ insurance (**AVS**), disability insurance (IV), income compensation (EO), unemployment insurance, accident insurance and health insurance. In addition there are occupational pensions and family allowances. People who work pay in part of their wages, and the employer often pays half.

The AVS was introduced in 1948 and pays a **pension** to people who have reached the retirement age of 65. It also helps widows, widowers and orphans. It is financed mainly on a **pay-as-you-go basis**: the contributions of people working today are paid straight back out as pensions. The AVS contribution is 8.7 per cent of wages, paid half by employees and half by employers (as of 2026). Since 2026 there has also been a 13th AVS pension payment each year.

Since 1972 the **three-pillar principle** has been in the Federal Constitution. The first pillar is the AVS, which is meant to cover basic living needs. The second pillar is **occupational pension provision** with a pension fund; there each person builds up their own savings, and the minimum conversion rate is 6.8 per cent (as of 2026). The third pillar is private provision, such as tax-advantaged saving in pillar 3a.

Since 1996 everyone in Switzerland has had to be insured with a health insurance fund. You pay a **premium** every month. When you go to the doctor, you first pay yourself up to the **deductible** you have chosen; for adults the lowest is 300 francs a year (as of 2026). After that you pay a share of 10 per cent; for children there is no deductible. People who earn little can receive a reduction in their premiums.

People who are employed are insured against **accidents** through their employer. Unemployment insurance pays money if you lose your job and are looking for a new one. The IV supports people who cannot work, or can only work partly, because of an illness or disability. The EO replaces part of your wages during military service and during maternity or paternity leave.

People who work pay AVS contributions from 1 January after their 17th birthday. Even people who do not work, such as students, must pay contributions from the age of 20. Missing years of contributions lead to a lower pension later. On your salary statement you can see exactly how much has been deducted for social insurance.

begriffe.erklaerung: Money you receive regularly, for example in old age.
The contributions of working people are paid directly as pensions to retired people.
The amount you pay yourself each year before the health insurance fund pays.
The regular amount you pay for an insurance.
An institution with which employees save for their old age; the second pillar.

gewusst: The AVS is Switzerland’s most important social insurance and pays out billions in pensions every year.
For children there is no deductible in health insurance.
The idea of an AVS existed long before 1948, but several earlier attempts failed.

teile.einleitung: Zurich is the largest city in Switzerland and lies at the lower end of Lake Zurich, where the Limmat leaves the lake. The city is an important centre for business, banking, science and culture, and its old town with the Grossmünster is known around the world.
wichtigste: Zurich is the largest city in Switzerland, with around 440,000 inhabitants (2024).
The city lies on Lake Zurich, from which the Limmat flows through the city.
The Grossmünster with its two towers is the landmark of the old town.
At the spring festival of Sechseläuten, the Böögg, a snowman made of cotton wool, is burnt.
Zurich is not the capital, because the Confederation has its seat in Bern.
Zurich is home to ETH Zurich, the university and the Swiss stock exchange SIX.
Zurich main station is the busiest railway station in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Zurich lies in the north of Switzerland at the northern end of **Lake Zurich**. The **Limmat** flows out of the lake right through the city, and the Sihl flows into it. Above the city rises its local mountain, the **Uetliberg**, 871 metres high. In clear weather you can see the Alps from there. The city is also the capital of the canton of Zurich, the most populous canton in Switzerland.

The Romans already had a customs post here called **Turicum**, which is where the name Zurich comes from. In the Middle Ages Zurich became a rich trading town, and in 1351 it joined the Confederation. From 1519 **Huldrych Zwingli** preached at the Grossmünster and brought the Reformation to Zurich. In the 19th century Zurich became a business metropolis through industry, the railway and banks.

The **Grossmünster** with its two towers is the best-known church in the city and was built from about 1100. Opposite, on the other bank of the Limmat, stands the **Fraumünster**, famous for its coloured stained-glass windows by Marc Chagall. St Peter’s Church has the largest church clock face in Europe, almost 9 metres across. In the old town, narrow lanes, old guild houses and the Niederdorf invite you to stroll.

**Sechseläuten** is the big spring festival of the Zurich guilds and takes place in April. The guild members parade through the city in historical costumes. In the evening the **Böögg** is set alight on the Sechseläutenplatz; it is a snowman made of cotton wool with fireworks in its head. The custom says that the faster its head explodes, the better the summer will be.

Zurich is the most important financial centre in Switzerland; large banks have their headquarters on the **Bahnhofstrasse** and at Paradeplatz. The Swiss stock exchange SIX Swiss Exchange is also in Zurich. **ETH Zurich** was founded in 1855 and is one of the best universities in the world; Albert Einstein studied there. Zurich Airport in Kloten is the largest airport in the country.

**Zurich Zoo** has the Masoala Hall, a recreated rainforest from Madagascar. The National Museum right next to the main station shows the history of Switzerland. In summer many people swim at the lake and river baths, the Badis, and in the Limmat. Every year in August the Street Parade with music floats winds around the lake basin.

begriffe.erklaerung: The river that flows out of Lake Zurich through the city of Zurich.
An old association of craftsmen or merchants that today mainly keeps up customs.
A snowman made of cotton wool that is burnt at Sechseläuten and is meant to drive away winter.
The renewal of the Church in the 16th century, led in Zurich by Zwingli.

gewusst: The clock face of St Peter’s Church is so big that the minute hand is almost 6 metres long.
The name Zurich goes back to the Roman Turicum, which was a customs post around 2000 years ago.
Zurich may be the largest city in Switzerland, but the Federal Assembly meets in Bern.

teile.einleitung: Silvesterchlausen is an old custom in the Appenzell Hinterland in the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden. On New Year’s Eve groups of Chläuse with large bells go from farm to farm and wish people a happy New Year.
wichtigste: The Silvesterchläuse belong to the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden.
They go round on 31 December and on the old New Year’s Eve, 13 January.
The Chläuse wear heavy bells and rows of small round bells on their bodies.
They sing a Zäuerli, a natural yodel without words.
A group of Chläuse is called a “Schuppel”.
There are beautiful, ugly and beautiful-ugly Chläuse.

abschnitte.text: The Chläuse wear large **bells** on their chest and back, or many small round **bells** on a belt. When they walk and jump, these ring loudly. In front of a house they stand in a circle and sing a **Zäuerli**. This is a slow natural yodel without words. Afterwards they wish the people living there a happy New Year and are often given something to drink or a small present.

The **beautiful Chläuse** (schöne Chläuse) wear magnificent headdresses and hats with little figures, scenes from village life and glittering decorations. The **ugly Chläuse** (wüeschte Chläuse) look wild. Their costumes are made of fir twigs, moss, leaves and other natural materials. The **beautiful-ugly Chläuse** (schö-wüeschte Chläuse) are a mixture of both. The men often work on the costumes for months.

The custom takes place on 31 December and once more on **13 January**. This is the “old New Year’s Eve”. The reason lies in the calendar: in the past the **Julian calendar** was used. When people changed to today’s calendar, the days shifted. That is why some municipalities went on celebrating the New Year according to the old date. In Urnäsch you can experience both dates.

Silvesterchlausen is one of the best-known customs in Switzerland. Many spectators come to the **Appenzell region** especially for it. For the families in the Hinterland, though, it is above all part of their own lives. Fathers pass on their knowledge of the costumes and the Zäuerli to the younger ones. Children also go round in their own groups.

gewusst: A large bell can weigh several kilograms, and a Chlaus often carries two of them.
Silvesterchlausen is on the list of living traditions in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has more than 1500 lakes, from small mountain lakes to large lakes with steamers. Many of them were formed by glaciers in the ice age. The lakes supply drinking water, are popular places for outings and shape the landscape.
wichtigste: The largest lake that Switzerland has a share of is Lake Geneva.
Lake Neuchâtel is the largest lake that lies entirely within Switzerland.
As well as Switzerland, Germany and Austria also border Lake Constance.
Lake Maggiore lies partly in Switzerland and partly in Italy.
Interlaken lies between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz.
Most large lakes were formed by glaciers in the ice ages.
There are more than 1500 lakes in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: **Lake Geneva**, in French Lac Léman, is the largest lake that Switzerland has a share of, at around 580 square kilometres. About three fifths of it belong to Switzerland and the rest to France. **Lake Constance** lies between Switzerland, Germany and Austria. In the south, Switzerland shares **Lake Maggiore** and Lake Lugano with Italy.

The largest lake that lies entirely within Switzerland is **Lake Neuchâtel** at the southern foot of the Jura. It borders the cantons of Neuchâtel, Vaud, Fribourg and Bern. Other well-known lakes are Lake Lucerne with its many arms, Lake Zurich and Lake Walen. In the Bernese Oberland lie Lake Thun and Lake Brienz, with the town of **Interlaken** between them.

Most large lakes formed after the **ice ages**. Huge glaciers carved out deep valleys and, as they melted, left behind ridges of rubble, the **moraines**. Water collected behind them and formed lakes. In the Alps there are also many small mountain lakes and artificial **reservoirs**, for example the Lac des Dix in the Valais.

Scheduled boats run on many lakes, and some of them are paddle steamers more than 100 years old. In summer many people swim, sail and paddle in the lakes. Many towns such as Zurich, Lucerne, Geneva and Lugano lie right by the water. In Geneva the Jet d’eau, a famous fountain, shoots water around 140 metres into the air.

**Drinking water** is taken from many lakes, for example from Lake Zurich and Lake Constance. Fish such as whitefish, perch and lake trout live in the lakes. In the past some lakes were badly polluted by sewage. Thanks to sewage treatment plants, the water quality today is usually very good.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ridge of stones and rubble left behind by a glacier.
An artificial lake behind a dam, often for producing electricity.
A lake that belongs to several countries.
A long, cold period when large parts of the land were covered by glaciers.

gewusst: There is no firmly agreed border between the three countries on Lake Constance.
Lake Lucerne has so many arms that from above it looks almost like a cross.
Lake Maggiore is the deepest lake that Switzerland has a share of.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Alps are the great high mountain range in the south and east of Switzerland. With mighty peaks, glaciers and mountain lakes, they shape the image of Switzerland all over the world. They are home to rare animals and plants and an important area for tourism and energy.
wichtigste: The Alps cover around 60 per cent of the area of Switzerland.
The highest mountain in Switzerland is the Dufourspitze in the Monte Rosa massif, at 4634 metres.
A glacier is a large mass of ice that slowly flows down the valley.
The Great Aletsch Glacier is the largest glacier in the Alps.
The ibex, with its large curved horns, lives in the Alps.
The marmot whistles loudly when danger threatens.
Edelweiss is a well-known alpine flower with white, woolly flowers.

abschnitte.text: In the Swiss Alps there are many **four-thousanders**, mountains more than 4000 metres high. The highest is the **Dufourspitze**, at 4634 metres, on the border with Italy. The best known is the **Matterhorn** near Zermatt, at 4478 metres, which is world-famous because of its shape. In the Bernese Oberland the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau stand side by side.

A **glacier** forms when, over many years, more snow falls than melts and it is pressed together into ice. Because of its weight, the ice flows very slowly down the valley. The **Great Aletsch Glacier** in the Valais is around 20 kilometres long and the largest glacier in the Alps. Because of global warming, the glaciers have been melting heavily for decades.

The **ibex** climbs very skilfully on steep rocks; at one time it was wiped out in Switzerland and was reintroduced from 1911. The **marmot** lives in burrows, whistles loudly when there is danger and hibernates for a long time in winter. Other alpine animals are the chamois, the golden eagle and the bearded vulture. The rock ptarmigan also lives here and changes its plumage to white in winter.

The higher you climb, the colder it gets and the fewer plants grow. Lower down there are deciduous and coniferous forests; from about 2000 metres is the **tree line**. Above it there are alpine pastures with flowers such as gentian, alpine rose and **edelweiss**. Edelweiss has white, woolly flowers that protect it from the cold and strong sunshine.

The Alps are a popular destination for hiking, climbing and skiing; well-known resorts are Zermatt, St Moritz and Grindelwald. Many reservoirs in the Alps supply electricity from **hydropower**. Important transport routes lead from north to south over passes and through tunnels. At 57 kilometres, the Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world.

In the Alps, avalanches, falling rocks and mudflows can be dangerous. The weather in the mountains can change very quickly. That is why you should take good shoes, warm clothing and enough to drink. Avalanche warnings are issued by the Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research in Davos.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mountain that is higher than 4000 metres.
A large mass of ice made of pressed snow that slowly flows down the valley.
The height above which trees can no longer grow.
A long, deep sleep with which some animals get through the winter.

gewusst: The Jungfraujoch, with its railway station at 3454 metres, is often called the “Top of Europe”.
Marmots sleep for up to half a year in their burrow.
The Alps are still being formed today, because the African plate is pushing against the European plate.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is often called the water tower of Europe. Large rivers such as the Rhine, the Rhône, the Inn and the Ticino rise in its mountains and carry their water to four different seas. The longest river that runs entirely within Switzerland is the Aare.
wichtigste: At about 290 kilometres, the Aare is the longest river that lies entirely within Switzerland.
The Rhine flows from the Grisons via Basel to the North Sea.
The Rhône rises in the Valais and flows into the Mediterranean.
The Inn from the Engadine carries its water via the Danube to the Black Sea.
The Ticino flows via the Po into the Adriatic Sea.
The Limmat flows right through the city of Zurich.
Many rivers supply electricity from hydroelectric power stations.

abschnitte.text: A lot of rain and snow falls in the Alps, and many **glaciers** store water. This gives rise to streams and rivers that flow away in every direction. That is why Switzerland is called the **water tower of Europe**. Swiss water reaches the North Sea, the Mediterranean, the Black Sea and the Adriatic. At the Lunghin Pass in the Engadine there is a watershed between three of these seas.

The **Rhine** is formed in the Grisons from the Vorderrhein and the Hinterrhein. It flows through Lake Constance, plunges over the Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen and leaves Switzerland at Basel heading for the North Sea. The **Aare** rises at the Aare glaciers in the Bernese Oberland. It flows through Lake Brienz and Lake Thun, loops around the old town of Bern and joins the Rhine at Koblenz in the canton of Aargau. Shortly before that, at Brugg, it takes in the Reuss and the Limmat.

The **Rhône** rises at the Rhône Glacier, flows through the Valais and crosses Lake Geneva. After Geneva it flows through France to the Mediterranean. The **Inn** begins in the Upper Engadine and flows via Austria to Passau, where it joins the Danube. The **Ticino** flows through the canton of Ticino into Lake Maggiore and later into the Po, which flows into the Adriatic.

Many towns lie on rivers, because water used to be important for trade, mills and drinking water. Zurich lies on the **Limmat**, which comes out of Lake Zurich. Lucerne lies on the Reuss, Bern and Solothurn on the Aare, Basel on the Rhine and Geneva on the Rhône. Bridges such as the Chapel Bridge in Lucerne became landmarks.

Around 60 per cent of Swiss electricity comes from **hydropower**, for example from river power stations and reservoirs. In the past many rivers were straightened to gain land and prevent flooding. Today stretches of river are being **restored to nature** again so that fish and other animals have more habitat. In summer, river swimming is very popular, for example in the Aare in Bern or in the Rhine in Basel.

begriffe.erklaerung: The place where a river rises.
The place where a river flows into another river, a lake or the sea.
A line that decides in which direction the water flows away.
Making a river more natural again so that plants and animals can live better.

gewusst: The Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen is one of the waterfalls in Europe with the most water.
In summer many people in Bern let themselves drift through the city with the current of the Aare.
The Aare, Reuss and Limmat meet near Brugg; this area is also called the Wasserschloss, the water castle.

t1vsfe1u.t: Coats of arms of the Swiss cantons
