teile.einleitung: Each of the 26 Swiss cantons has its own coat of arms, which you can see on flags, number plates and buildings. The coats of arms show animals, saints, stars or simple areas of colour and often tell us something about the history of the canton.
wichtigste: All 26 cantons have their own coat of arms with fixed colours and pictures.
The coat of arms of the canton of Valais shows 13 stars on a white and red background.
The coat of arms of the canton of Uri shows a black bull’s head with a red nose ring.
The Glarus coat of arms shows St Fridolin as a pilgrim.
In the coat of arms of Schaffhausen a black ram is leaping.
The canton of Thurgau has two golden-yellow lions in its coat of arms.
Many coats of arms are several hundred years old and date from the Middle Ages.

abschnitte.titel: What is a coat of arms?
abschnitte.text: A coat of arms is a sign of recognition in the shape of a shield. In the Middle Ages knights carried such signs on their shields so that they could be recognised in armour. Later towns, countries and families adopted their own coats of arms. The study of coats of arms is called **heraldry**. It has strict rules, for example about which colours may stand next to each other.

abschnitte.titel: Animals in the coats of arms
abschnitte.text: Many cantons have an animal in their coat of arms that is meant to show strength or courage. Bern has a black **bear** on a yellow diagonal band, and both Appenzells also show a bear. Uri bears a black bull’s head, the **Uri bull**, on a yellow background. Schaffhausen shows a leaping black ram, and in the Thurgau coat of arms two yellow lions stand on a background divided into green and white.

The Valais shows **13 stars**, which stand for the old districts of the canton, the Zenden. Obwalden and Nidwalden bear keys, a sign of the apostle Peter. Glarus is the only canton that shows a person, namely **St Fridolin**, the patron saint of the land of Glarus. He is shown as a traveller with a staff, a book and a pilgrim’s bag.

Some coats of arms have no picture at all and show only areas of colour. Zurich is divided diagonally into white and blue, Lucerne vertically into blue and white. Zug has a blue band on a white background, and Solothurn is red at the top and white at the bottom. Such simple coats of arms are very old and easy to recognise on flags from far away. Schwyz shows a small white cross on a red background, which later became the **Swiss cross**.

The **Basel crosier** in the coat of arms of Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft recalls the crosier of the bishops of Basel. The Geneva coat of arms shows half an eagle and a key, signs of the Empire and the bishop. Vaud bears the words “Liberté et Patrie”, that is freedom and fatherland. The canton of Jura was only created in 1979 and so has the youngest cantonal coat of arms.

abschnitte.titel: Coats of arms in everyday life
abschnitte.text: You can see cantonal coats of arms on car number plates, next to the Swiss coat of arms. They hang as flags on town halls and are hung on many houses on 1 August. Sports clubs, police cars and the letterheads of authorities also often bear the **cantonal coat of arms**. So a coat of arms shows at a glance which canton something belongs to.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science and art of designing and explaining coats of arms.
The shape, usually like a knight’s shield, on which the coat of arms is painted.
Old districts in the Valais, which the stars in the Valais coat of arms recall.
A stylised bishop’s staff in the coat of arms of the two Basels.

gewusst: The coat of arms of St Gallen shows a bundle of eight rods with an axe, which is meant to stand for the unity of the municipalities.
Together with the flag of the Vatican, the Swiss flag is one of the few square national flags in the world.
The bear in the Bernese coat of arms goes back to the legend that Duke Berchtold V of Zähringen named the town after the first animal he killed.

teile.einleitung: Italian-speaking Switzerland includes the canton of Ticino and a few valleys in the south of the Grisons. People speak Italian there. The area lies south of the Alps and has a mild climate.
wichtigste: Italian is one of the four national languages of Switzerland.
In Ticino, Italian is the only official language.
In the Grisons, Italian is one of three official languages.
Italian is spoken there, for example, in the Mesolcina, the Bregaglia and the Val Poschiavo.
The capital of Ticino is Bellinzona and the largest town is Lugano.
South of the Alps it is often warmer and sunnier.

abschnitte.text: Italian-speaking Switzerland lies in the south of the country. The largest part is the **canton of Ticino**, where Italian is the only **official language**. In addition there are valleys in the **Grisons**, which are called **Italian Grisons**. They include the Mesolcina, the Val Calanca, the Bregaglia and the Val Poschiavo. In the Grisons, German, Romansh and Italian are official languages.

The capital of Ticino is **Bellinzona**, known for its three castles, which are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The largest town is **Lugano** on Lake Lugano. **Locarno** on Lake Maggiore is famous for its **film festival** in summer. Ticino has been a canton in its own right since 1803. Before that, the area was ruled for a long time by the Confederates.

Ticino lies **south of the Alps**. That is why the climate is milder than in the north. Palm trees, camellias and fig trees grow on Lake Maggiore and Lake Lugano. In the north of the canton, however, there are also high mountains and wild valleys such as the **Verzasca Valley**. Many people from German-speaking Switzerland go on holiday here.

The Alps lie between German-speaking Switzerland and Ticino. The link over the **Gotthard** is important. Today trains run through the **Gotthard Base Tunnel**, one of the longest railway tunnels in the world. It opened in 2016. This means you can get from Zurich to Lugano in a short time. For cars there is the Gotthard road tunnel and the pass.

gewusst: Ticino has its own university, the Università della Svizzera italiana.
Most of Lake Maggiore lies in Italy; only its northern end belongs to Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Switzerland shows a white cross on a red background. It is square, which makes it almost unique in the world. You can see it on houses, on mountains, at sporting events and especially on 1 August.
wichtigste: The Swiss flag is red with a white cross in the middle.
It is square; only the flag of Vatican City has the same shape.
The arms of the cross are one sixth longer than they are wide.
On the national holiday, 1 August, a particularly large number of people put up flags.
A flag flown at half-mast shows that people are mourning someone.
In flag throwing, a large flag is skilfully thrown through the air.
The Red Cross emblem is the Swiss flag with the colours reversed.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss flag shows a free-standing **white cross** on a red background. The cross does not touch the edge. Its four arms are the same length and each is one sixth longer than it is wide. The flag is **square**. On ships at sea, however, Switzerland uses a rectangular version.

The white cross on red goes back to the banner of the canton of **Schwyz**. As early as the Middle Ages, Confederate warriors wore white crosses on their clothing as a sign of recognition. It was made the official coat of arms of the Confederation in 1815. With the founding of the federal state in 1848, the flag became the symbol of the whole country. The Federal Assembly fixed the exact measurements of the cross in 1889.

On the **national holiday** on 1 August, many people decorate balconies, gardens and streets with flags and paper lanterns. Fans also wave the flag at sporting events such as football matches. A Swiss flag also flies on many mountain peaks. If a flag is only raised to **half-mast**, that is halfway up, it is a sign of mourning.

**Flag throwing** is an old Swiss custom. A large, often square flag on a short pole is swung, passed around the body and thrown high into the air. The flag throwers perform set figures and often appear to the sound of yodelling or alphorns. You can see the custom at yodelling festivals, Swiss wrestling festivals and on 1 August.

abschnitte.titel: The Swiss cross as a brand
abschnitte.text: The **Swiss cross** stands for quality all over the world, for example on penknives or watches. For a product to carry the cross, by law a large part of it must come from Switzerland. This is called **Swissness**. In 1863, in honour of Switzerland and its founder Henry Dunant, the Red Cross chose the Swiss flag with the colours reversed as its protective emblem.

begriffe.erklaerung: When a flag hangs only halfway up, as a sign of mourning.
A symbol that stands for a country, a canton or a family.
A country’s birthday, in Switzerland 1 August.
Rules on when a product may be described as Swiss.

gewusst: Apart from Switzerland, only Vatican City has a square national flag.
Each of the 26 cantons also has its own flag with its own coat of arms.
The flag of the canton of Schwyz still shows a small white cross in the upper corner today.

teile.einleitung: The “Röstigraben” is not a real ditch that you can find on a map. The word is used with a wink to describe the differences between German-speaking Switzerland and western Switzerland, the Romandie.
wichtigste: The Röstigraben separates opinions and habits, not landscapes.
It runs roughly along the language border between German and French.
The name comes from rösti, which is seen as a typical dish of German-speaking Switzerland.
The Röstigraben often becomes visible in popular votes.
Bilingual places such as Biel/Bienne and Fribourg lie right on the language border.
In the Romandie it is called “barrière de rösti” in French.

abschnitte.text: **Rösti** is a dish of grated potatoes fried golden brown in the pan. It is seen as typical of German-speaking Switzerland. That is why the imaginary line between the language regions was jokingly called the **Röstigraben**, the rösti ditch. A ditch is really a hollow in the ground. Here it is only an image for a division in people’s minds.

Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. The **language border** between German and French runs right across the country from north to south. Some cantons, such as Bern, Fribourg and Valais, are **bilingual**. In towns such as Biel/Bienne you hear both languages in the street. The River Saane (Sarine) is often named as an image for the Röstigraben, because the language border in the canton of Fribourg runs near it.

People talk about the Röstigraben especially often after **popular votes**. Sometimes the Romandie votes quite differently from German-speaking Switzerland. A well-known example is the vote on the **EEA** in 1992: western Switzerland clearly said yes, while German-speaking Switzerland mostly said no. In many other votes, though, there is no Röstigraben. Then town and country vote differently, whatever language people speak.

Switzerland is called a **nation by will**. This means it holds together even though the people speak different languages. At school children learn a second national language. The SRG broadcasting company makes radio and television for all language regions. So the Röstigraben usually remains a joke rather than a real split.

gewusst: There is a similar joking word for the border with Italian-speaking Switzerland: the “Polentagraben”, the polenta ditch.
Around two thirds of the people in Switzerland speak German as their main language; French-speaking Switzerland is much smaller.

teile.einleitung: The Knabenschiessen is a traditional folk festival in Zurich. Every year in September young people compete at shooting. Around the shooting range at the Albisgüetli there is one of the largest funfairs in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Knabenschiessen takes place every year in September in Zurich.
It lasts from Saturday to Monday.
Young people shoot at targets; today both girls and boys.
Whoever shoots best becomes shooting king or shooting queen.
There is a large funfair (Chilbi) at the Albisgüetli.
Girls have been allowed to take part since 1991.

abschnitte.text: The Knabenschiessen, literally the “boys’ shoot”, is a **shooting competition** for young people. It has a long tradition going back to earlier centuries. At that time young men were supposed to learn how to handle weapons. Today it is above all a **sporting competition** and a big festival. The shooting takes place under supervision at the shooting range at the **Albisgüetli**.

In the past only **boys** were allowed to take part, hence the name. Since **1991** **girls** have also been admitted. Young people from Zurich and the surrounding area aged about 13 to 17 can take part. Several thousand young people take part every year. Whoever scores the most points is crowned **shooting king** or **shooting queen**.

A large **Chilbi**, a funfair, takes place around the shooting range. There are roundabouts, roller coasters, a big wheel and many stalls with Magenbrot, candyfloss and grilled sausages. Many families visit the funfair even if they do not shoot themselves. It is one of the largest funfairs in Switzerland. In good weather the grounds are very crowded.

The Knabenschiessen takes place on the **second weekend in September**. The **Monday** is a special day in the city of Zurich: many pupils and many employees have the day off. The shooting king or queen is also announced on the Monday. For many people in Zurich, the festival is a fixed part of the year.

gewusst: The Knabenschiessen is one of the largest folk festivals in the city of Zurich.
The Albisgüetli lies at the foot of the Uetliberg, Zurich’s local mountain.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has four national languages. In most cantons only one of them is an official language. But some cantons are officially multilingual: Bern, Fribourg and Valais officially use two languages, and the Grisons even three.
wichtigste: Bern, Fribourg and Valais are bilingual in German and French.
The Grisons is trilingual: German, Romansh and Italian.
Official language means that the authorities use this language.
In the canton of Bern the majority speak German, in Fribourg French.
Biel/Bienne is the largest bilingual town in Switzerland.
The four national languages are German, French, Italian and Romansh.

abschnitte.text: An **official language** is the language in which the authorities, courts and schools work. Laws and forms are available in this language. In a multilingual canton you can contact the administration in any of the official languages. Usually, however, one language is mainly used in each **municipality**. Which one that is depends on what people there have traditionally spoken.

In the **canton of Bern** the great majority speak **German**. But in the **Bernese Jura** in the north of the canton people speak **French**. The town of **Biel**, in French **Bienne**, is fully bilingual. There you hear both languages in the street, and the street signs are bilingual. Biel is the largest bilingual town in Switzerland.

In the **canton of Fribourg** the majority speak **French**, but in the east of the canton German. The town of Fribourg is called **Freiburg** in German and lies close to the language border. It is similar in the **Valais**: in the **Upper Valais** people speak German, in the **Lower Valais** French. The language border runs roughly near Sierre and Leuk. The capital Sion is called Sitten in German.

The **Grisons** is the only trilingual canton. Its official languages are **German**, **Romansh** and **Italian**. Romansh is spoken, for example, in the Engadine and the Surselva. Italian is spoken in the southern valleys such as the Mesolcina and the Val Poschiavo. In many parts of the canton German is the main language.

gewusst: The imaginary border between German- and French-speaking Switzerland is jokingly called the “Röstigraben”, the rösti ditch.
The University of Fribourg offers many courses in German and in French.

teile.einleitung: Traditions are old customs and practices that a community keeps up over many generations. In Switzerland they include music, sport, festivals and food, which are often connected with the seasons and with life in the countryside. Many of these customs are still alive today and attract thousands of people.
wichtigste: The alphorn is a very long wooden musical instrument that is played in the mountains.
In Swiss wrestling, two men or women wrestle in sawdust.
Fondue is a cheese dish that people eat together from one pot.
On 6 December the Samichlaus, the Swiss St Nicholas, visits the children.
At the Alpabzug in autumn, the cows come down from the alp to the valley.
Many customs differ from region to region.
The Basel Fasnacht is part of UNESCO’s intangible cultural heritage.

abschnitte.text: The **alphorn** is a wind instrument made of wood, usually spruce, and often more than three metres long. In the past herdsmen used it to communicate over long distances; today it is played mainly at festivals. **Yodelling** is also part of Swiss folk music: the voice switches quickly between a low chest voice and a high head voice. Often a Ländler band with a Schwyzerörgeli, a small Swiss accordion, plays along.

**Schwingen** is a Swiss kind of wrestling that takes place in a round ring of sawdust. The wrestlers wear short trousers made of strong twill, by which they grab each other. The aim is to put the opponent on his back with both shoulders. Every three years the Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival takes place, and the winner becomes **wrestling king**. Other traditional sports are Hornussen and stone putting.

For **fondue**, cheese is melted with white wine in a pot, the caquelon, and everyone dips pieces of bread into it with long forks. A well-known mixture is “moitié-moitié”, half and half, of Gruyère and Vacherin fribourgeois. Raclette, rösti and Bircher muesli are also considered typically Swiss. Many dishes come from farmhouse cooking, in which people had to manage with few ingredients.

On 6 December the **Samichlaus** visits the children, often accompanied by the Schmutzli in a dark robe. The children recite a little rhyme and receive nuts, mandarins and gingerbread. In Küssnacht am Rigi, the Klausjagen takes place on the evening before St Nicholas Day, with huge glowing headdresses. In the Engadine, at **Chalandamarz** on 1 March, children drive away winter with bells.

abschnitte.titel: Going up to and coming down from the alp
abschnitte.text: In early summer the farmers take their cows up to the alp, where the animals eat fresh grass all summer. In autumn comes the **Alpabzug**, called Désalpe in French. The cows are decorated with flowers and large bells and walk down to the valley in a festive procession. In many villages there is a market with cheese and music.

The **Basel Fasnacht** begins on the Monday after Ash Wednesday at 4 o’clock in the morning with the Morgestraich, when all the lights are switched off. In Lucerne too, people celebrate loudly with Guggenmusik bands and masks. In Zurich, at **Sechseläuten** in spring, a snowman made of cotton wool, the Böögg, is burnt on a pile of wood. The faster its head explodes, the better the summer is supposed to be.

begriffe.erklaerung: Old customs and practices that are handed down over many generations.
The winner of the Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival.
The pot made of ceramic or cast iron in which fondue is prepared.
A mountain pasture where cattle graze in summer.
The companion of the Samichlaus, who wears a dark cloak.

gewusst: In good weather an alphorn can be heard several kilometres away.
At the Unspunnen Festival, a stone weighing more than 80 kilograms is thrown as far as possible.
The Böögg at Sechseläuten is filled with fireworks, which is why its head explodes with a loud bang.

teile.einleitung: The political system of Switzerland is unique in the world. It combines federalism, direct democracy and a government in which all the big parties work together. Its basis is the Federal Constitution, which sets out who has which tasks and rights.
wichtigste: Switzerland is a democratic federal state with the Confederation, cantons and municipalities.
Parliament consists of the National Council and the Council of States.
The 200 National Council seats are shared out among the cantons according to their resident population.
The Federal Council is the seven-member government and works according to the principle of collegiality.
With a motion, parliament can instruct the Federal Council in a binding way to present a law.
In the consultation procedure, cantons, parties and associations can comment on draft laws.
Parliament cannot remove the Federal Council during its term of office through a vote of no confidence.

abschnitte.text: The basis of the state is the **Federal Constitution**. The first dates from 1848, when Switzerland became a federal state; the present one has applied since 2000. Power is divided between three levels: the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities. It is also divided between parliament, government and the courts. Thanks to initiatives and referendums, the people have the last word on many decisions.

The federal parliament is called the **Federal Assembly** and consists of two chambers with equal rights. The National Council has 200 seats, which are shared out among the cantons according to their resident population. The Council of States has 46 seats, two per canton and one per former half-canton. Both chambers must agree to a law. If differences between them remain, a **conciliation conference** looks for a compromise.

The government of Switzerland is the **Federal Council**, with seven members who each head a department. They are elected by the United Federal Assembly for four years. Every year a different member takes on the office of President of the Confederation. According to the **principle of collegiality**, all members represent the government’s decisions together to the outside world, even if they held a different opinion. Parliament cannot remove the Federal Council during its term of office through a vote of no confidence.

A new law can be started by the Federal Council, by parliament, by a canton or through a popular initiative. With a **motion**, parliament instructs the Federal Council in a binding way to present a draft law. Then comes the **consultation procedure**, in which cantons, parties and associations give their views. After that the National Council and the Council of States debate the draft one after the other. Finally the people can still vote on it with a referendum.

In Switzerland there is no clear division between government and opposition. The largest parties are represented together in the Federal Council; this is called **concordance**. Because the people can call a referendum at any time, the parties try to find solutions with as broad support as possible. This system is considered slow but very stable.

From the age of 18, Swiss citizens may vote and take part in elections at federal level. They can also get involved in parties, hand in petitions or stand for office. Many offices in municipalities are carried out in the **militia system**, that is alongside a job. Young people can gain their first political experience in youth parliaments.

begriffe.erklaerung: The most important law of Switzerland, which sets out the basic rules of the state.
The rule that all members of the Federal Council represent decisions together.
An instruction from parliament to the Federal Council to prepare a law.
A procedure in which interested parties can give their opinion on a draft law.
The cooperation of all the big parties in the government.

gewusst: The President of the Confederation is not head of state alone but only the first among equals in the Federal Council.
Officially Switzerland has no capital city; Bern is called the federal city.
Federal councillors are almost always re-elected; voting them out is very rare.

teile.einleitung: The history of Switzerland tells how a small alliance of valley communities in the Alps became a modern federal state. Many events, such as the Federal Charter of 1291 or the legend of William Tell, are still part of the picture Switzerland has of itself today. Historical facts and legends are mixed together.
wichtigste: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden made the Federal Charter in 1291.
In the Battle of Morgarten in 1315 the Confederates defeated the Habsburgs.
According to legend, Arnold Winkelried sacrificed himself at the Battle of Sempach in 1386.
In 1798 the French set up the Helvetic Republic as a unitary state.
The Sonderbund War of 1847 was Switzerland’s last civil war.
In 1848 Switzerland became a modern federal state.
William Tell is said to have shot the apple off his son’s head in Altdorf.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages, the areas of present-day Switzerland belonged to various rulers; the **Habsburgs** in particular were powerful. At the beginning of August 1291, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden formed an alliance and promised to help each other. This document is called the **Federal Charter** and is kept today in the Museum of the Swiss Charters of Confederation in Schwyz. That is why 1 August is the national holiday. According to legend, the founders swore the alliance on the **Rütli meadow** on Lake Lucerne.

According to legend, **William Tell** had to shoot an apple off his son’s head in Altdorf because he had not saluted the hat of the bailiff Gessler. Whether Tell really lived has not been proven. In 1315 the Confederates defeated the Habsburgs at the Battle of **Morgarten**. In 1386 they won the Battle of Sempach, where, according to legend, Arnold Winkelried sacrificed himself. Gradually other places such as Lucerne, Zurich and Bern joined the alliance.

In 1515 the Confederates lost the Battle of **Marignano** and afterwards withdrew from the great wars. From 1519 Huldrych Zwingli preached the **Reformation** in Zurich, and later John Calvin in Geneva. The Confederation split into Reformed and Catholic places, which fought each other several times. In the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, independence from the Holy Roman Empire was recognised.

abschnitte.titel: The Helvetic Republic and a new order
abschnitte.text: In 1798 French troops marched in and founded the **Helvetic Republic**, a unitary state on the French model. The old places lost their power, and all citizens were to have equal rights. In 1803 Napoleon gave Switzerland a federal order again with the Act of Mediation. At the **Congress of Vienna** in 1815, Switzerland received most of its present borders and its neutrality was recognised.

In 1847 the Catholic cantons of the Sonderbund fought against the liberal cantons; this was the **Sonderbund War**. It lasted only a few weeks, and General Dufour made sure that there were few victims. In 1848 Switzerland got a Federal Constitution and became a **federal state** with Bern as the federal city. Later came important steps such as women’s suffrage in 1971, the founding of the canton of Jura in 1979 and joining the UN in 2002.

begriffe.erklaerung: The members of the alliance, who promised each other help by swearing an oath.
The document of 1291 with which Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden formed an alliance.
A story handed down over time that may have a true core but is not precisely proven.
A state in which several member states join together under a common government.

gewusst: 1 August was only celebrated as the national holiday from 1891, and it has only been a public holiday off work since 1994.
The Federal Charter of 1291 is written in Latin.
The famous play about William Tell was written by the German poet Friedrich Schiller in 1804.

teile.einleitung: A referendum is a popular vote on a decision of parliament. In Switzerland it allows the voters to have the last word on laws and changes to the constitution. It is one of the most important tools of direct democracy.
wichtigste: There is the mandatory and the optional referendum.
Every change to the Federal Constitution is automatically subject to the mandatory referendum.
The mandatory referendum needs a popular majority and a majority of the cantons.
An optional referendum needs 50,000 signatures within 100 days.
8 cantons together can also call a referendum.
In an optional referendum against a federal law, a popular majority is enough.
The optional referendum on laws has existed at federal level since 1874.

abschnitte.text: The word **referendum** comes from Latin and means roughly “that which must be referred back”. So a decision of parliament is put to the people to decide. The people can accept or reject it. Unlike a popular initiative, in a referendum the people do not propose anything new but say yes or no to something parliament has decided.

For certain proposals the people must always vote; this is called a **mandatory referendum**. This includes every change to the Federal Constitution. Joining organisations for collective security or supranational communities is also included. A proposal is only accepted if it wins a **popular majority** and a **majority of the cantons**, that is a majority of voters and a majority of the cantons.

The **optional referendum** can be called against new federal laws, many federal decrees and certain international treaties. This requires 50,000 valid signatures from voters within 100 days of official publication. Alternatively, 8 cantons together can call the **cantonal referendum**. In the vote a popular majority is then enough. If no referendum is called, the law comes into force without a vote.

Sometimes a law has to apply very quickly, for example in a crisis. Then parliament can declare it **urgent** and bring it into force immediately. If such a law has no basis in the constitution, it must be put to the people and the cantons within a year. Otherwise it ceases to be valid after a year.

The mandatory constitutional referendum has existed since the founding of the federal state in 1848. With the total revision of the Federal Constitution in 1874, the optional referendum on laws was added. One of the best-known votes took place on 6 December 1992: the people and the cantons narrowly rejected joining the **European Economic Area** (EEA). Turnout was exceptionally high at the time, almost 79 per cent.

begriffe.erklaerung: More than half of all valid votes in the whole country are yes votes.
The majority of the cantons have said yes.
Voluntary; it only takes place if someone asks for it.
Compulsory; it must take place in any case.
A referendum called jointly by at least 8 cantons.

gewusst: The cantonal referendum was successful for the first time at federal level only in 2003, on a tax package.
Switzerland holds more national popular votes than almost any other country in the world.
Most laws come into force without a vote, because nobody calls a referendum.

teile.einleitung: Swiss inventions are things and ideas that were developed by people in Switzerland. We come across many of them every day, from the hook-and-loop fastener on our shoes to the vegetable peeler in the kitchen. Switzerland is still considered a particularly inventive country today.
wichtigste: George de Mestral from western Switzerland invented the hook-and-loop fastener.
Alfred Neweczerzal patented the vegetable peeler in 1947.
Daniel Peter invented milk chocolate in Vevey in 1875.
The chemist Jacques Brandenberger invented the transparent film cellophane in 1908.
Karl Elsener is considered the inventor of the Swiss Army knife.
The World Wide Web was created at CERN near Geneva in 1989.
Relative to its population, Switzerland registers a particularly large number of patents.

abschnitte.text: The engineer **George de Mestral** from Vaud got the idea after a walk with his dog. Burrs were stuck in its fur, holding on with tiny hooks. De Mestral examined them under the microscope and copied the principle. This led to the **hook-and-loop fastener**, which was patented in the 1950s. The brand name Velcro is made up of the French words velours (velvet) and crochet (hook).

The chocolatier **Daniel Peter** from Vevey mixed milk into chocolate in 1875 and so invented **milk chocolate**. He was helped by the powdered milk of his neighbour Henri Nestlé. A few years later, in 1879, Rodolphe Lindt in Bern invented the conche, a machine that makes chocolate melt smoothly. Since then Swiss chocolate has been world-famous.

The cutler **Karl Elsener** from Ibach in the canton of Schwyz supplied knives to the Swiss army from 1891. From these he developed the **Swiss Army knife** with several tools; his company is called Victorinox today. The **vegetable peeler** “Rex” is also a Swiss invention; Alfred Neweczerzal patented it in 1947. With its movable blade you can peel potatoes and carrots thinly.

The chemist **Jacques Brandenberger** invented **cellophane**, a transparent film made of cellulose, in 1908. He originally wanted to make tablecloths stain-resistant. Today cellophane is used to wrap food and presents. Another well-known Swiss invention is the typeface Helvetica, which was created in 1957 and can be seen on signs and logos all over the world.

At the research centre **CERN** near Geneva, the British researcher Tim Berners-Lee developed the **World Wide Web** in 1989. At the universities ETH Zurich and EPFL Lausanne, many new technologies are still being researched today. Swiss companies develop medicines, watches, robots and machines. In worldwide comparisons of innovation, Switzerland has been in one of the top places for years.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something new that someone has thought up and built.
A right that allows an inventor to be the only one to use their invention for a certain time.
A machine that stirs chocolate mass for a long time and so makes it smooth.
A substance from plants from which, for example, paper and cellophane are made.

gewusst: The idea for the hook-and-loop fastener came from burrs that got stuck in a dog’s fur.
The Rex vegetable peeler has been sold millions of times and has looked almost the same for decades.
The World Wide Web was created at a research centre for particle physics.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland lies in the middle of Europe and has five neighbouring countries: Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein. It is closely linked with each of these countries through history, language and the economy. It shares its longest border with Italy and its shortest with Liechtenstein.
wichtigste: Switzerland borders Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein.
Switzerland’s longest border is with Italy.
It shares its shortest border with Liechtenstein.
In Liechtenstein people pay with Swiss francs.
The canton of Geneva borders France almost all the way round.
The national languages German, French and Italian are also spoken in the neighbouring countries.
Except for Liechtenstein, all the neighbouring countries are members of the European Union.

abschnitte.text: In the north Switzerland borders **Germany**, mainly along the Rhine and on Lake Constance. Near Basel, Switzerland, Germany and France meet at the point where the three countries’ borders meet. The canton of Schaffhausen lies mostly north of the Rhine and is almost completely surrounded by Germany. The German village of **Büsingen** is an exclave that is entirely surrounded by Swiss territory. Germany is Switzerland’s most important trading partner.

In the west Switzerland borders **France**. The border runs through the Jura and Lake Geneva into the Alps at the Mont Blanc massif. In western Switzerland, the Romandie, people speak French, as in France. Every day many people commute from France to work in Switzerland, especially to Geneva and Basel.

Switzerland shares its longest border, around 740 kilometres, with **Italy**. It runs high across the Alps, over peaks such as the Matterhorn and the Dufourspitze. Ticino and parts of the Grisons are Italian-speaking. On Lake Lugano lies the Italian village of **Campione d’Italia**, which is completely surrounded by Swiss territory.

In the east Switzerland borders **Austria** and **Liechtenstein**. At about 41 kilometres, the border with Liechtenstein is the shortest and mostly follows the Rhine. Liechtenstein is closely linked with Switzerland: it has used the **Swiss franc** since 1924 and forms a common customs area with it. Among other things, Switzerland shares Lake Constance with Austria; there is no firmly agreed border on the lake.

Switzerland is not a member of the **European Union**, but it works closely with it. Since 2008 it has been part of the **Schengen Area**, which is why there are usually no longer regular passport checks at the borders. Goods, however, are still checked at customs. Many people like to go shopping abroad where things are cheaper; this is called shopping tourism.

begriffe.erklaerung: An area of one country that is completely surrounded by the territory of another country.
A place where the borders of three countries meet.
A group of European countries between which you can usually travel without passport checks.
A check on goods brought across a border, and a charge on them.

gewusst: Swiss customs rules apply in Büsingen, and people usually pay with francs, even though the village belongs to Germany.
Germany, Austria and Switzerland have never agreed on an exact border on Lake Constance.
The border with Italy runs over many glaciers, which have to be measured again and again because they are melting.

teile.einleitung: In a popular vote, the voters decide directly on an issue, for example on a law or a change to the constitution. In Switzerland such votes take place much more often than in almost any other country. They are the heart of direct democracy.
wichtigste: As a rule, federal votes take place on 4 dates a year.
The people must always vote on changes to the Federal Constitution.
A popular initiative needs a popular majority and a majority of the cantons to be accepted.
In a vote there are 23 cantonal votes in total.
In 2007 the canton of Glarus was the first to introduce a voting age of 16.
At federal level you may vote from the age of 18.
Most people vote by post.

abschnitte.text: In a **popular vote**, the voters say yes or no to a proposal. The reason is either a **referendum**, that is a decision of parliament, or a **popular initiative**, that is a proposal from the people. Votes are held at the level of the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities. At federal level they usually take place on four Sundays a year.

abschnitte.titel: Popular majority and majority of the cantons
abschnitte.text: For a federal law a **popular majority** is usually enough, that is more yes votes than no votes in the whole country. Changes to the constitution and popular initiatives also need a **majority of the cantons**. There are 23 cantonal votes in total, because six cantons each have only half a vote. A majority of the cantons requires at least 12 cantonal votes.

A few weeks before voting Sunday, all voters receive the papers at home. These include a booklet with the **Federal Council’s explanations** and the arguments of both sides. You can vote by post or go to the polling station on Sunday and put your ballot paper in the ballot box. Today most people vote by post.

At federal level, Swiss citizens aged 18 and over may vote. In the canton of **Glarus**, young people have been allowed to vote on cantonal and municipal matters from the age of 16 since 2007. Foreign residents have no right to vote at federal level, but they do in some cantons and municipalities. Women only received the right to vote and stand for election at federal level in 1971.

In the cantons of Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden there is still the **Landsgemeinde**. There the voters gather once a year in the open air in a square. They vote by raising their hands, and the votes are estimated rather than counted. The Landsgemeinde is one of the oldest forms of democracy.

begriffe.erklaerung: Having the right to take part in votes.
The majority of the cantons that agree to a proposal.
The vote of one canton when the majority of the cantons is worked out.
The share of voters who actually voted.
An open-air assembly at which people vote by raising their hands.

gewusst: Since 1848 Swiss voters have voted on well over 600 federal proposals.
In the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, women only received the cantonal right to vote in 1990, through a ruling by the Federal Supreme Court.
Turnout in federal votes is often less than half of those entitled to vote.

teile.einleitung: The Jungfraujoch is a saddle between the Jungfrau and Mönch mountains in the Bernese Alps. The highest railway station in Europe is here, at around 3450 metres above sea level. The place is also called “Top of Europe”.
wichtigste: The Jungfraujoch lies between the Jungfrau and the Mönch.
The station is at around 3450 metres above sea level.
It is the highest railway station in Europe.
The Jungfrau Railway runs up from the Kleine Scheidegg through a tunnel.
The railway was completed in 1912.
From the top you can look down on the Great Aletsch Glacier.

abschnitte.text: The **Jungfrau Railway** starts at the **Kleine Scheidegg**. From there it first runs briefly in the open air and then into a long **tunnel**. This leads through the **Eiger** and the **Mönch** to the Jungfraujoch. Construction began in 1896 and took around 16 years. In 1912 the railway finally reached its destination.

The idea came from the Zurich businessman **Adolf Guyer-Zeller**. Many workers, mainly from Italy, blasted and dug the tunnel through hard rock. The work was hard and dangerous, and there were accidents. On the way there are stops with windows in the rock, such as **Eismeer** station. There you can look out at glaciers and rock faces.

On the Jungfraujoch there are viewing platforms, an **Ice Palace** with figures made of ice, and passages in the glacier. High up stands the **Sphinx**, an observatory with a viewing terrace. Researchers measure the air and the weather there. Because the air is thin at this height, you should move slowly. There is snow here even in summer.

From the Jungfraujoch you look down on the **Great Aletsch Glacier**. It is the longest glacier in the Alps. Because of the warmer climate it has been getting shorter for many years. Since 2001 the area has been part of the **UNESCO World Heritage Site** “Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch”. The Jungfraujoch lies exactly on the border between the cantons of **Bern** and **Valais**.

gewusst: The Sphinx on the Jungfraujoch is one of the highest research stations in Europe.
The tunnel of the Jungfrau Railway is around seven kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: Lake Geneva is the largest lake that Switzerland has a share of. It lies between Switzerland and France and is shaped like a crescent moon. In French it is called Lac Léman.
wichtigste: At around 580 square kilometres, Lake Geneva is one of the largest lakes in Central Europe.
About 60 per cent of the lake belongs to Switzerland and the rest to France.
In French the lake is called Lac Léman.
The Rhône flows into Lake Geneva and out again at Geneva.
Chillon Castle stands right on the shore near Montreux.
The vineyards of Lavaux on the northern shore are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The lake is up to about 310 metres deep.

abschnitte.text: **Lake Geneva** lies in the south-west of Switzerland between the cantons of Geneva, Vaud and Valais and France. It is about 73 kilometres long and has an area of around 580 square kilometres. This makes it bigger than Lake Constance. The surface of the lake is about 372 metres above sea level. The deepest point measures around 310 metres.

The most important river flowing in is the **Rhône**, which comes from the Valais. It enters at the eastern end of the lake and brings a lot of sand and glacial mud with it. At Geneva it leaves the lake again towards France. Because the lake is so big, it takes on average about eleven years for its water to be completely replaced. Strong winds such as the **Bise** sometimes blow over the lake.

**Chillon Castle** near Montreux stands on a rock right in the water and is one of the most visited castles in Switzerland. On the northern shore between Lausanne and Montreux lie the steep vineyards of **Lavaux**, which have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007. In Montreux a statue recalls the singer Freddie Mercury. In Geneva the Jet d’eau shoots up out of the lake.

On the Swiss shore lie towns such as **Geneva**, Lausanne, Vevey and Montreux. On the French southern shore are Évian-les-Bains and Thonon-les-Bains. The International Olympic Committee has its headquarters in Lausanne, and the food company Nestlé in Vevey. The region is densely populated and is often called the Arc lémanique.

The boats of the **CGN** operate on the lake, including several historic paddle steamers from around 1900. Many people commute by boat between France and Lausanne. In summer you can swim, sail and go stand-up paddleboarding. Fish such as whitefish and perch live in the lake and are often served in restaurants.

begriffe.erklaerung: The French name for Lake Geneva.
A river or stream that flows into a lake.
A ship driven by large paddle wheels on its sides.
An especially valuable place that UNESCO protects.

gewusst: Lake Geneva is a little bigger than Lake Constance, which makes it the largest lake on the edge of the Alps.
Lake Geneva sometimes has standing waves called seiches, in which the water level sloshes back and forth.
Chillon Castle was used as a prison for a long time and became famous through a poem by Lord Byron.

teile.einleitung: Geneva is the second largest city in Switzerland and lies at the south-western end of Lake Geneva. The city is known all over the world because the UN, the Red Cross and many other international organisations have their headquarters here. Its landmark is the Jet d’eau, a huge fountain in the harbour.
wichtigste: Geneva is the capital of the canton of the same name in the far south-west of Switzerland.
Most people in Geneva speak French.
The Jet d’eau shoots water around 140 metres into the air.
Geneva is an important seat of the UN and many international organisations.
There is a famous flower clock in the English Garden.
In December Geneva celebrates the Escalade with pots made of chocolate.
Geneva is almost completely surrounded by France.

abschnitte.text: Geneva lies where the **Rhône** leaves Lake Geneva. The canton of Geneva borders France almost all the way round and only borders the canton of Vaud along a narrow stretch. The city has about 200,000 inhabitants and the whole canton around half a million (as of 2024). Many people commute to work in Geneva from France every day; they are called **cross-border commuters**.

In the 16th century Geneva became a centre of the **Reformation**, shaped by the theologian John Calvin. That is why Geneva was also called the Protestant Rome. In 1602 troops of the Duke of Savoy tried to capture the city at night but were driven back. The festival of the **Escalade** recalls this every year in December. Geneva only became a Swiss canton in 1815.

The European headquarters of the UN is in the **Palais des Nations** in Geneva. The International Committee of the Red Cross, the World Health Organization WHO and the World Trade Organization WTO also have their home here. In the past the League of Nations had its seat in Geneva. The research centre **CERN** is also near Geneva. That is why important international conferences often take place in Geneva.

The **Jet d’eau** is the most famous fountain in Switzerland and shoots water about 140 metres into the air. In the English Garden on the lakeshore is the **flower clock**, whose face is made of thousands of flowers. The old town with St Peter’s Cathedral and the Reformation Wall in the Parc des Bastions are also worth seeing. In front of the Palais des Nations stands a huge chair with a broken leg, which recalls the victims of landmines.

At the **Escalade** children dress up and parade through the old town. According to legend, in 1602 Mère Royaume poured hot vegetable soup over the attackers. That is why today people smash a pot made of **chocolate**, the so-called marmite, filled with marzipan vegetables. The youngest and the oldest members of the family break the pot together.

Geneva is an important centre for **banks**, commodity trading and luxury watches. Well-known watch brands such as Patek Philippe and Rolex have their headquarters here. Geneva Airport is the second largest in Switzerland. The famous motor show also took place in Geneva for many years.

begriffe.erklaerung: A movement in the 16th century from which the Reformed Church emerged.
People who live in one country and work in the neighbouring country.
A Geneva festival that recalls the defeat of an attack in 1602.
The large complex of UN buildings in Geneva.

gewusst: The Jet d’eau originally started out as a pressure-release valve at a waterworks.
The philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau was born in Geneva in 1712.
The flower clock in the English Garden recalls Geneva’s long tradition of watchmaking.

teile.einleitung: With a popular initiative, citizens in Switzerland can themselves propose changing the Federal Constitution. If enough people sign, the proposal goes to the people. In this way people outside parliament can also bring new ideas into politics.
wichtigste: A federal popular initiative needs 100,000 valid signatures.
The signatures must be collected within 18 months.
The popular initiative for a partial revision of the Federal Constitution has existed since 1891.
An initiative must respect the unity of subject matter.
If an initiative breaks mandatory international law, it must be declared invalid.
Since 1987 there has been a deciding question when an initiative and a direct counter-proposal are put to the vote.
On 3 March 2024 the initiative for a 13th AVS pension payment was accepted.

abschnitte.text: A **popular initiative** is a proposal from the people to change or add to the Federal Constitution. A group of voters forms an **initiative committee** and writes a text. Then they collect signatures in the street, by post or at events. If enough valid signatures come together, the people must vote on it.

A federal popular initiative needs 100,000 valid **signatures** from voters. These must be collected within 18 months. The municipalities check that the people who signed really are entitled to vote. Then the committee hands in the signatures to the Federal Chancellery in Bern.

An initiative must respect the **unity of subject matter**, which means there must be a real connection between its parts. It must also respect the unity of form. If it breaks mandatory rules of international law, such as the ban on torture, the Federal Assembly must declare it invalid. This has happened only very rarely so far.

The Federal Council and parliament give a recommendation and can make a **counter-proposal**. An **indirect counter-proposal** is a change in the law that partly meets the demand. A direct counter-proposal is a separate constitutional text that is voted on at the same time. Since 1987 you may say yes to both and answer a **deciding question**, which determines which proposal applies if both are accepted. The committee often withdraws its initiative if the counter-proposal is enough for it.

The popular initiative for a partial revision of the constitution was introduced in 1891. Only about one in ten initiatives is accepted by the people and the cantons. Well-known accepted initiatives are the Alpine Initiative of 1994 to protect the Alps from transit traffic, and the initiative for a **13th AVS pension payment**, which was accepted on 3 March 2024. Rejected initiatives often have an effect too, because they start a debate.

begriffe.erklaerung: The group of people who start a popular initiative and are responsible for it.
The rule that all parts of an initiative must belong to the same topic.
A proposal by the Federal Council and parliament as an alternative to an initiative.
An extra question that decides which proposal applies if two are accepted.
Rules that apply between the states of the world.

gewusst: The first federal popular initiative to be accepted dates from 1893.
Before 1987 you were not allowed to vote yes twice on an initiative and a counter-proposal.
Several years often pass between handing in an initiative and the vote.

teile.einleitung: The Council of States is one of the two chambers of the Swiss parliament. The cantons are represented in it; each canton sends one or two people to Bern. Together with the National Council it forms the Federal Assembly.
wichtigste: The Council of States has 46 members.
It is also called the small chamber.
Most cantons have 2 seats; Basel-Stadt and five other cantons have 1 seat each.
The cantons decide how the members of the Council of States are elected.
For a new federal law, both councils must agree.
The National Council and the Council of States have equal rights.
The members are elected for four years.

abschnitte.titel: What is the Council of States?
abschnitte.text: The Swiss parliament is called the **Federal Assembly** and consists of two chambers. The **National Council**, with 200 members, represents the people; the **Council of States**, with 46 members, represents the cantons, which used to be called Stände (estates). Because it has fewer members, the Council of States is also called the small chamber. This division is called the **two-chamber system**; Switzerland introduced it in 1848 on the model of the USA.

Each canton has the same number of seats in the Council of States, no matter how many people live there. 20 cantons have 2 seats each. The six cantons of Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden have 1 seat each. So the small canton of Uri has as much weight as the large canton of Zurich.

The cantons decide for themselves how their members of the Council of States are elected. In almost all cantons the **majority system** applies, so whoever receives the most votes is elected. The cantons of Jura and Neuchâtel use proportional representation. In Appenzell Innerrhoden the member of the Council of States is elected at the Landsgemeinde. The elections usually take place every four years together with the National Council elections.

Together with the National Council, the Council of States debates new **laws**, the federal budget and international treaties. A law is only passed if both councils agree. If they do not agree, the proposal goes back and forth between the councils in the **procedure for resolving differences**. Together, as the United Federal Assembly, both councils elect the Federal Council and the federal judges.

The Council of States meets in the Council of States chamber in the Federal Palace in Bern. Parliament normally meets four times a year for a three-week session. The members are not a full-time parliament; many also have another job. This system is called a **militia parliament**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of parliament that debates and votes separately.
An electoral system in which whoever receives the most votes is elected.
The time during which parliament meets and debates.
A parliament whose members often also have a job alongside politics.

gewusst: Until 2014 the Council of States voted by show of hands; since then it has voted electronically.
The small canton of Uri, with around 38,000 inhabitants, has as many seats in the Council of States as the canton of Zurich with more than 1.5 million.
The cantons used to be called Stände, which is where the German name Ständerat comes from.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is famous for its banks and insurance companies. People talk about the Swiss financial centre when they mean all the companies that trade in money, manage it or insure it. Zurich and Geneva in particular are among the most important financial centres in the world.
wichtigste: The Swiss financial centre includes banks, insurance companies, the stock exchange and many asset managers.
Since 2009 FINMA has supervised banks, insurance companies and stock exchanges.
The Swiss National Bank aims to keep prices stable.
In March 2023 UBS took over Credit Suisse.
Bank deposits are protected up to 100,000 francs per customer and bank.
The Swiss Market Index (SMI) includes the 20 largest shares on the Swiss stock exchange.
Since 2018 Switzerland has automatically exchanged tax data with many countries.

abschnitte.text: There are around 240 banks in Switzerland, including **big banks**, cantonal banks, Raiffeisen banks and private banks. The largest is UBS, with its headquarters in Zurich. Almost every canton has its own **cantonal bank**, which is often guaranteed by the canton. Many people from abroad have their wealth managed by Swiss banks. Switzerland is one of the largest centres in the world for managing wealth across borders.

The **Swiss National Bank** (SNB) was founded in 1907 and has offices in Bern and Zurich. It issues the banknotes and steers the country’s monetary policy. Its most important aim is **price stability**, meaning that money keeps its value. From 2011 to January 2015 it defended a minimum exchange rate of 1.20 francs per euro. When it dropped this minimum rate, the franc suddenly became much stronger.

Shares in companies are bought and sold on the stock exchange. The Swiss stock exchange is called **SIX Swiss Exchange** and is based in Zurich. The most important share index is the **SMI**, which includes the 20 largest companies, such as Nestlé, Novartis and Roche. If the SMI rises, these shares have on average gained in value.

So that banks handle their customers’ money carefully, there is **FINMA**, the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority. It was set up in 2009 and is based in Bern. If a bank goes bust, **deposit protection** covers savings up to 100,000 francs per customer and bank. Large insurance companies such as Zurich, Swiss Life or the reinsurer Swiss Re also come from Switzerland.

For a long time **banking secrecy** was a trademark of Switzerland; it was written into the Banking Act in 1934. Because it was also misused for tax evasion, Switzerland came under international pressure. Since 2018 it has exchanged account data with partner countries through the **automatic exchange of information**. In 2023 the long-established Credit Suisse fell into a serious crisis and was taken over by UBS in March.

Even children can open their own **savings account** at a bank. Money is safer in an account than in a piggy bank. A bank statement shows you how much money has come in and gone out. Compare interest rates and fees before you choose a bank.

begriffe.erklaerung: A marketplace where shares and other securities are traded.
A small part of a company that you can buy.
When goods cost roughly the same over time and money keeps its value.
A safeguard so that savers get their money back if a bank goes bust.

gewusst: Paradeplatz in Zurich is seen as the heart of the financial centre, because UBS and the former Credit Suisse have their headquarters there.
Every Swiss banknote carries a signature of members of the National Bank’s management.
The financial sector produces about a tenth of Switzerland’s total economic output.

teile.einleitung: Every car in Switzerland has a number plate. It shows in which canton the vehicle is registered. The two letters at the front stand for the canton.
wichtigste: Each canton has a two-letter code.
AI stands for Appenzell Innerrhoden, AR for Appenzell Ausserrhoden.
A number follows the code.
At the back of the car, the Swiss coat of arms and the cantonal coat of arms are shown.
The canton’s road traffic office issues the plates.
In Switzerland the number belongs to the keeper, not to the car.

abschnitte.text: A Swiss number plate is **white** with **black lettering**. First comes the **canton code**, for example ZH for Zurich or BE for Bern. Then follows a **number** with up to six digits. The rear plate also shows the **Swiss coat of arms** and the **coat of arms of the canton**. The front plate is narrower and has no coats of arms.

All 26 cantons have their own **two-letter** code. Some are easy to guess, such as **UR** for Uri or **AG** for Aargau. With the two Appenzells you have to look carefully: **AI** stands for **Appenzell Innerrhoden** and **AR** for **Appenzell Ausserrhoden**. Other examples are GR for the Grisons, TI for Ticino and VS for Valais. The VS comes from the French name Valais.

The plates are issued by the canton’s **road traffic office**. In Switzerland the number is tied to the **keeper**, that is the person who owns the vehicle. If someone buys a new car, they can keep the old number. Anyone who has two cars but only ever drives one at a time can use an **interchangeable plate**. If you move to another canton, you need a new plate.

Not all plates are white. **Mopeds** have a small **yellow** plate, and tractors and other farm vehicles a **green** one. Diplomats’ vehicles often have the letters **CD**. Army vehicles carry an **M** instead of a canton code. Some people pay a lot of money for very short numbers such as ZH 10, because some cantons **auction** such numbers.

gewusst: Several tens of thousands of francs have already been paid at auctions for particularly low numbers.
When a car travels abroad, the code CH shows that it comes from Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The law of Switzerland is the whole set of rules that apply to living together in Switzerland. It sets out what is allowed and forbidden, how contracts work and how disputes are settled in court. Because Switzerland is a federal state, there is law from the Confederation, from the cantons and from the municipalities.
wichtigste: Swiss law belongs to the legal family of continental European law, also called civil law.
The most important rules are in written laws, for example in the Federal Constitution, the Civil Code and the Criminal Code.
The main author of the Swiss Civil Code (ZGB) was the lawyer Eugen Huber.
The Swiss Criminal Code came into force in 1942.
According to Article 2 of the Civil Code, everyone must act in good faith.
Since 2011 a single Criminal Procedure Code and Civil Procedure Code have applied throughout Switzerland.
The highest court is the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne; the Federal Administrative Court sits in St Gallen.

abschnitte.text: Law means the binding rules that everyone must keep to. Unlike the rules of a game, the state can also enforce the law, for example with courts and the police. A distinction is made between **public law**, which regulates the relationship between the state and people, and **private law**, which regulates the relationships between people. Swiss law belongs to **civil law**, which means that the most important rules are written down in codes of law.

At the very top is the **Federal Constitution**; the present version has applied since 2000. Below it come the federal laws and the ordinances of the Federal Council. Each canton also has its own constitution and its own laws, for example for schools, police and taxes. Municipalities may also issue their own rules, for example regulations on rubbish collection. Federal law takes precedence over cantonal law.

The **Civil Code (ZGB)** was drawn up by the lawyer **Eugen Huber** and came into force in 1912. It sets out, for example, when you come of age, how marriage and family are organised and who inherits something. Article 1 of the Civil Code says: if the law contains no rule, the court decides according to the rule it would make if it were the legislator. Article 2 requires everyone to act in **good faith**, that is honestly and fairly. The Civil Code was so successful that Turkey adopted it almost completely in 1926.

The **Criminal Code** sets out which acts are crimes and what punishments they carry. It was accepted by the people in 1937 and came into force in 1942; before that each canton had its own criminal law. For children and young people aged 10 and over there is a special **juvenile criminal law**, in which education and protection come first. Since 2011 a single Criminal Procedure Code and Civil Procedure Code have regulated how court proceedings take place.

Disputes first go before the courts of the cantons. Anyone who disagrees with a judgment can often appeal. The highest court in Switzerland is the **Federal Supreme Court** in Lausanne; part of it works in Lucerne. There is also the Federal Criminal Court in Bellinzona, the **Federal Administrative Court** in St Gallen and the Federal Patent Court, also in St Gallen.

You come across law every day, even if you do not notice it. When you buy an ice cream, you make a contract of sale, which is governed by the **Code of Obligations**. In Switzerland you come of age, and so have full legal capacity, at 18. Children may still make small purchases themselves with their pocket money.

begriffe.erklaerung: A written rule that was decided by parliament or the people and applies to everyone.
The principle that you must act honestly and fairly and must not trick others.
A legal system in which the most important rules are written down in large codes of law.
The highest court in Switzerland, based in Lausanne.
The age from which you may make contracts yourself; in Switzerland 18.

gewusst: With some changes, the Swiss Civil Code still applies in Turkey today, because it was adopted there in 1926.
Many Swiss laws exist in three equally valid language versions: German, French and Italian.
Before the Criminal Code came into force in 1942, the same act could be punished very differently depending on the canton.

teile.einleitung: The separation of powers means that power in a state is divided between different bodies. Nobody should be allowed to make laws, carry them out and judge them all at the same time. This protects people from the abuse of power.
wichtigste: State power is divided into the legislature, the executive and the judiciary.
Montesquieu described this idea in 1748 in his work “De l’esprit des lois” (The Spirit of the Laws).
In Switzerland the Federal Assembly is the legislature, the Federal Council the executive and the Federal Supreme Court the judiciary.
The Federal Supreme Court has its main seat in Lausanne.
The United Federal Assembly elects the judges of the Federal Supreme Court.
Because of incompatibility, nobody may be a federal councillor and a member of the National Council at the same time.
The vertical separation of powers divides power between the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities.

abschnitte.titel: What is the separation of powers?
abschnitte.text: A state has three big tasks: making laws, carrying out laws and judging disputes. With the **separation of powers**, different bodies take on these tasks. The law-making power is called the **legislature**, the power that carries out laws the **executive**, and the judging power the **judiciary**. The three powers check each other. This means that no single person and no single group can decide everything.

As far back as ancient times, philosophers thought about how power could be limited. The English thinker John Locke wrote about it in the 17th century. But the idea became famous through the French philosopher **Montesquieu**, who described it in 1748 in his book “De l’esprit des lois”. His thoughts influenced the US Constitution of 1787 and later the Swiss **Federal Constitution** of 1848 too.

abschnitte.titel: The three powers at federal level
abschnitte.text: The legislature is the **Federal Assembly** with the National Council and the Council of States. The executive is the **Federal Council**, the seven-member government, supported by the federal administration. The judiciary is formed mainly by the **Federal Supreme Court** in Lausanne, Switzerland’s highest court. There are also other federal courts, such as the Federal Criminal Court in Bellinzona and the Federal Administrative Court in St Gallen.

So that the powers really are separate, the rule of **incompatibility** applies. A member of the Federal Council may not sit in the National Council or the Council of States at the same time. Federal judges may not hold any office in parliament or the government either. If someone from parliament is elected to the Federal Council, they must give up their seat in parliament.

In Switzerland the separation of powers is not completely strict. The United Federal Assembly elects both the Federal Council and the **federal judges**. In addition, according to Article 190 of the Federal Constitution, the Federal Supreme Court may not set aside federal laws, even if they contradict the constitution. Parliament and ultimately the people are meant to have the last word. This rule is debated again and again.

As well as the division into three powers, there is the **vertical separation of powers**. This means that power is also divided between the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities. Each level has its own parliaments, governments and in some cases its own courts. Thanks to direct democracy, the people are also an important check on the authorities.

begriffe.erklaerung: The law-making power, that is the parliament.
The power that carries out laws, that is the government and the administration.
The judging power, that is the courts.
The rule that you may not hold two particular offices at the same time.

gewusst: As well as Lausanne, the Federal Supreme Court also has a site in Lucerne.
Federal judges are elected for six years.
Montesquieu’s book “De l’esprit des lois” was first published in Geneva in 1748.

teile.einleitung: By international standards the towns and cities of Switzerland are rather small, but they are very varied. The largest city is Zurich, and the federal city is Bern. Each town has its own history, language and sights.
wichtigste: Zurich is the largest city in Switzerland.
Bern is the federal city, with the Federal Palace.
Chur is the capital of the canton of the Grisons.
St Gallen has the famous old Abbey Library.
Locarno in Ticino lies on Lake Maggiore.
Biel in the canton of Bern is bilingual; people speak German and French.
In Swiss statistics a town is usually a municipality with more than 10,000 inhabitants.

abschnitte.text: The largest city is **Zurich**, with more than 400,000 inhabitants (as of about 2024). Then come Geneva, Basel, Lausanne and Bern. Other large towns are Winterthur, Lucerne, St Gallen, Lugano and Biel. Around the cities lie large **urban areas** where many commuters live.

**Bern** is the federal city; parliament and the Federal Council work here in the Federal Palace. Bern’s old town with its arcades and the Zytglogge clock tower has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983. Zurich is the most important business centre and lies on Lake Zurich. It is home to ETH Zurich, many banks and the largest railway station in Switzerland.

**Geneva** is an international city where the UN, the Red Cross and many other organisations have their seat. **Basel** lies on the Rhine on the border with Germany and France and is known for pharmaceutical companies, museums and the Fasnacht. The International Olympic Committee has its seat in Lausanne on Lake Geneva. These cities show how important Switzerland is for the world.

In **St Gallen** stands the abbey precinct with the cathedral and the **Abbey Library**, one of the oldest libraries in the world. The abbey precinct has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983. **Chur** is the capital of the canton of the Grisons and is considered one of the oldest towns in Switzerland. From here the Rhaetian Railway runs into the valleys of the Grisons.

In Ticino lie Lugano on Lake Lugano and **Locarno** on Lake Maggiore. Every August a famous film festival takes place in Locarno, at which films are shown in the open air on the Piazza Grande. **Biel**, in French Bienne, is the largest bilingual town in Switzerland. Street signs there are in both languages, and Biel is a centre of the watch industry.

begriffe.erklaerung: The city where the government and parliament have their seat; in Switzerland Bern.
The town where a canton’s government has its seat.
A town together with the surrounding municipalities that are closely connected with it.
The oldest part of a town, often with narrow lanes and historic houses.

gewusst: Officially Switzerland has no capital city; Bern is called the federal city.
In the Abbey Library of St Gallen you have to wear felt slippers to protect the old wooden floor.
Geneva is one of the cities with the most international organisations in the world.

teile.einleitung: Lucerne is a town in Central Switzerland on the shore of Lake Lucerne. With its wooden Chapel Bridge, the Water Tower and the Lion Monument, it is one of the most popular destinations in Switzerland. Its local mountain, Pilatus, rises above the town.
wichtigste: Lucerne is the capital of the canton of Lucerne and lies on Lake Lucerne.
The Chapel Bridge is one of the oldest covered wooden bridges in Europe.
Next to the Chapel Bridge, the octagonal Water Tower stands in the water.
The Lion Monument shows a dying lion carved into a rock.
Pilatus is Lucerne’s local mountain.
The Reuss flows through the town.
The Lucerne Fasnacht is one of the best known in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Lucerne lies where the **Reuss** flows out of Lake Lucerne. The town has about 85,000 inhabitants (as of 2024) and is the centre of Central Switzerland. All around, mountains such as **Pilatus** and the Rigi rise up. Lucerne is an important railway junction and a starting point for boat trips on the lake.

The **Chapel Bridge** was built in the 14th century and was part of the town’s fortifications. In the gable hang painted panels from the 17th century, which show stories from Lucerne and Switzerland. In 1993 a fire destroyed large parts of the bridge, but it was quickly rebuilt. Next to it stands the octagonal **Water Tower**, which used to serve as an archive, treasury and prison.

The **Lion Monument** is a huge dying lion carved into a rock face. It recalls Swiss Guards who died in Paris in 1792 during the storming of the Tuileries. The design is by the Danish sculptor Bertel Thorvaldsen, and the monument was unveiled in 1821. The writer Mark Twain called it one of the saddest works of art in the world.

**Pilatus** is about 2100 metres high and can be seen clearly from the town. The steepest **cogwheel railway** in the world runs up it, with a gradient of up to 48 per cent. According to an old legend, dragons are said to have lived on Pilatus. On the other side of the lake lies the Rigi, up which the first mountain railway in Europe ran in 1871.

The **Lucerne Fasnacht** begins on Dirty Thursday with the Urknall, the big bang, early in the morning. Then Guggenmusik bands march through the narrow streets playing loud brass music. In the Culture and Congress Centre **KKL** on the lake, designed by the architect Jean Nouvel, concerts take place, such as the Lucerne Festival. The Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne is the most visited museum in the country.

In the **old town** there are many houses with painted façades and pretty squares such as the Weinmarkt. The Musegg Wall with nine towers runs above the town. Another old wooden bridge is the Spreuer Bridge, with paintings of a Dance of Death. The Jesuit Church on the Reuss is considered one of the first large Baroque buildings in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bridge with a roof that protects the wood from rain.
A railway with a toothed wheel that grips a toothed rail so that it can climb steep mountains.
A carnival band that deliberately plays out of tune and loudly.
A structure or figure that recalls an event or people.

gewusst: The Chapel Bridge is about 200 metres long and crosses the Reuss at an angle.
According to legend, the name Pilatus is connected with the Roman governor Pontius Pilate.
The Musegg Wall has a tower clock that is allowed to strike one minute earlier than all the other clocks in the town.

teile.einleitung: Parties are groups of people with similar political ideas who want to have influence together. There are many parties in Switzerland, and the largest sit in parliament and in the government. Because no party has a majority on its own, they often have to find compromises.
wichtigste: The largest parties in Switzerland are the SVP, SP, FDP, The Centre, the Greens and the Green Liberals.
In the 2023 National Council elections the SVP was the party with the most votes.
From 1959 to 2003 the magic formula applied, with 2 FDP, 2 CVP, 2 SP and 1 SVP in the Federal Council.
The SVP emerged in 1971 from the Party of Farmers, Traders and Independents.
In 2009 the FDP and the Liberal Party merged to form FDP.The Liberals.
In 2021 The Centre was created from the CVP and the BDP.
Elisabeth Kopp of the FDP was the first woman elected to the Federal Council, in 1984.

abschnitte.text: A **party** is a group of people who have similar ideas about how a country should be run. Parties put forward candidates for elections and write **manifestos**. They also collect signatures for initiatives and referendums. Parties are often placed on a scale from left to right. On the left are parties that tend to want more balancing out by the state; on the right, parties that tend to stress more personal responsibility and less state.

The **SVP** (Swiss People’s Party) has been the party with the most votes since 1999 and campaigns, among other things, for independence and a strict migration policy. The **SP** (Social Democratic Party) is on the left and stresses social justice. FDP.The Liberals stands for freedom and the economy, and The Centre sees itself as a bridge-builder. The Greens and the Green Liberals put great importance on protecting the environment.

The largest parties are represented together in the Federal Council; this is called **concordance**. From 1959 to 2003 the **magic formula** applied: two seats for the FDP, two for the CVP, two for the SP and one for the SVP. In 2003 the SVP gained a second seat at the expense of the CVP. Today the SVP, SP and FDP each have two seats in the Federal Council and The Centre has one (as of 2026).

The party landscape keeps changing. The SVP was formed in 1971 from the Party of Farmers, Traders and Independents (**BGB**) and other parties. In 2009 the FDP and the Liberal Party of Switzerland joined together to form FDP.The Liberals. In 2021 the CVP and the BDP merged into the new party **The Centre**.

In National Council elections each party puts out a **list** of candidates. Voters may cross out names and add people from other lists; this is called **panachage**. Anyone who writes a name down twice is **cumulating** and gives that person two votes. This lets you decide very precisely whom you want to support.

In 1971 women gained the right to vote and to stand for election at federal level. In 1984 Elisabeth Kopp of the FDP was the first woman elected to the **Federal Council**. Since then women from almost all the big parties have sat on the Federal Council. Today about 40 per cent of the members of the National Council are women (as of 2023).

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of people with similar political ideas.
The cooperation of the big parties in the government.
Writing people from different party lists on one ballot paper.
Writing one person twice on the ballot paper so that they receive two votes.

gewusst: The magic formula lasted for 44 years, from 1959 to 2003.
