The SP is the oldest of today’s big parties in the Federal Council; it was founded in 1888.
In Switzerland most politicians do not work in politics full time but alongside their job.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland is small but very varied. It can be divided into regions by landscape, by language or by statistical area. From the glaciers of the Alps to the palm trees in Ticino, there are big differences over short distances.
wichtigste: Switzerland consists of three large landscape areas: the Jura, the Swiss Plateau and the Alps.
Around 60 per cent of the area belongs to the Alps.
The Swiss Plateau lies between the Jura and the Alps and is the most densely populated.
The French-speaking part of Switzerland is called the Romandie.
In Ticino, Italian is the only official language.
In the Grisons, Romansh is used as an official language.
The Federal Statistical Office divides Switzerland into 7 major regions.

abschnitte.text: In the north-west lies the **Jura**, a limestone range with long ridges and high plateaus, which makes up about a tenth of the area. In the middle lies the **Swiss Plateau**, a hilly landscape with lakes, fields and large towns, about 30 per cent of the area. In the south and east rise the **Alps**, which cover around 60 per cent of the area. The highest peaks, the large glaciers and many passes are there.

Although the Swiss Plateau makes up only about a third of the area, the great majority of the population lives there. Towns such as Zurich, Bern, Lausanne and Geneva lie here. Most factories, motorways and railway lines are also found on the Swiss Plateau. The fertile soil is good for growing crops.

The largest language region is **German-speaking Switzerland** in the north, centre and east. In the west lies the **Romandie**, where people speak French. Italian-speaking Switzerland includes the canton of Ticino and some valleys in the south of the Grisons. Romansh is spoken mainly in parts of the Grisons. The border between German-speaking Switzerland and the Romandie is jokingly called the **Röstigraben**.

For statistics, the Federal Statistical Office divides Switzerland into 7 major regions. They are called the Lake Geneva region, Espace Mittelland, North-western Switzerland, Zurich, Eastern Switzerland, Central Switzerland and Ticino. The Zurich major region consists only of the canton of Zurich, and Ticino only of the canton of Ticino. This makes it possible, for example, to compare wages, population or the economy of the regions.

South of the Alps, in Ticino, the climate is mild, and even palm trees and camellias grow. In the Alps, on the other hand, there is a lot of snow in winter, and on the highest peaks the ice never melts completely. The Alps act as a weather divide: it often rains on one side while the sun shines on the other. A well-known warm, dry wind blowing down the alpine valleys is the **Föhn**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hilly, densely populated landscape between the Jura and the Alps.
The French-speaking west of Switzerland.
A joking name for the language border between German-speaking Switzerland and the Romandie.
An area made up of several cantons that is grouped together for statistics.
A warm, dry wind that blows down into the alpine valleys.

gewusst: The canton of the Grisons is the only canton with three official languages: German, Romansh and Italian.
Although the Alps make up most of the area, only a small part of the population lives there.
The Röstigraben is named after rösti, a potato dish considered typical of German-speaking Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: In elections, voters decide which people represent them in parliaments and governments. In Switzerland elections are held at the level of the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities. The most important national elections are the elections to the National Council and the Council of States every four years.
wichtigste: The National Council is elected every four years; the next general elections take place in 2027 (as of 2026).
In most cantons the National Council is elected by proportional representation.
Adding names of candidates from other lists is called panachage.
In the 2023 National Council elections, the SVP won the largest share of the vote.
The Federal Council is not elected by the people but by the United Federal Assembly.
At federal level, anyone who is a Swiss citizen and at least 18 years old may vote.
The National Council has 200 seats, which are shared out among the cantons according to population.

abschnitte.text: At federal level the people elect the **National Council** and the Council of States. In the cantons the cantonal parliament and the cantonal government are elected by the people. In the municipalities people elect, for example, the municipal council and the school board. The **Federal Council**, that is the government of Switzerland, is elected by the United Federal Assembly.

In most cantons the National Council is elected by **proportional representation**. Each party receives as many seats as match its share of the votes. In cantons with only one National Council seat, such as Uri or Glarus, the majority system applies, so the person with the most votes is elected. The 200 seats are shared out according to population; the canton of Zurich has the most, with 36.

In the National Council election you choose a party’s **electoral list**, but you can change it. In **panachage** you add names of candidates from other lists. In **cumulative voting** you write a person’s name twice to give them an extra vote. You can also cross out names or fill in a blank list completely yourself.

There are many parties in Switzerland; the largest are the SVP, the SP, the FDP and The Centre. In the National Council elections in October 2023, the **SVP** won the largest share of the vote, about 28 per cent. The largest parties are represented together in the Federal Council; this is called **concordance**. No party has a majority on its own, so the parties have to look for compromises.

National Council elections take place every four years in October: the last in 2023, the next in 2027. As with votes, all voters receive their papers by post. Most people vote by post, but you can also go to the polling station. In the December after the election, the new parliament elects the Federal Council.

begriffe.erklaerung: An electoral system in which the seats are shared out according to the parties’ share of the vote.
Writing names of candidates from other parties on your own list.
Writing a person’s name twice on the list.
The largest parties govern together and look for compromises.

gewusst: On a National Council ballot paper in the canton of Zurich you can write up to 36 names.
From 1959 to 2003 the distribution of Federal Council seats among the parties stayed the same; it was called the magic formula.
Women in Switzerland have only been allowed to vote and be elected at federal level since 1971.

teile.einleitung: Federalism means that power in a state is divided between several levels. In Switzerland the Confederation, the 26 cantons and the municipalities share the tasks. That is why, for example, school holidays or taxes are not the same everywhere in the country.
wichtigste: Switzerland is a federal state made up of 26 cantons.
According to Article 3 of the Federal Constitution, the cantons are sovereign as far as the constitution does not limit their power.
According to the principle of subsidiarity, a task should be carried out by the smallest level that is able to do it.
Cantons can make agreements with each other, which are called concordats.
Since 2008 the NFA fiscal equalisation system has evened out differences between rich and poorer cantons.
For the majority of the cantons there are 23 cantonal votes in total.
In 1979 the Jura became part of the Confederation as the youngest canton.

abschnitte.text: The word **federalism** comes from the Latin foedus, which means alliance. A federal state is made up of member states that are allowed to regulate many things themselves. In Switzerland these are the **cantons**, which have their own constitutions, parliaments, governments and courts. Other federal states include Germany, Austria and the USA. Federalism allows regions with different languages and traditions to live together.

The **Confederation** looks after tasks that concern the whole country, such as the army, foreign policy, the post and the railways. The cantons are responsible among other things for schools, police and hospitals. The **municipalities** take care of local things such as nursery schools, rubbish collection or the water supply. Switzerland has about 2100 municipalities (as of 2025), and there are fewer each year because of mergers.

The **principle of subsidiarity** says that a task is done by the smallest level that can do it well. What a municipality can solve itself should not be taken over by the canton. Only when a task is too big does the next level up step in. This keeps decisions as close to the people as possible. Article 3 of the Federal Constitution also says that the cantons exercise all rights that have not been given to the Confederation.

Cantons often work together and make agreements for this, which are called **concordats**. One example is the HarmoS concordat, which brings compulsory schooling into line in many cantons. New cantonal constitutions must be guaranteed by the Federal Assembly. In this way the Confederation checks that they do not break federal law.

Each canton sets its own **taxes**, so people pay different amounts depending on where they live. Because some cantons are richer than others, there is **fiscal equalisation**. Since 2008 the new system of fiscal equalisation, NFA for short, has applied. It also made clear which tasks the Confederation and the cantons each pay for. Financially strong cantons such as Zug or Zurich pay in, and financially weaker ones receive money.

In the **Council of States** each canton has two seats and the former half-cantons have one each, 46 in total. In votes on the constitution, the majority of the cantons counts as well as the popular majority. Here 20 cantons have a whole vote and 6 cantons half a vote, which makes 23 **cantonal votes** together. The youngest canton is the Jura, which separated from the canton of Bern in 1979.

begriffe.erklaerung: A member state of Switzerland with its own constitution, government and parliament.
The principle that the smaller level takes on a task first.
An agreement between two or more cantons.
A system in which rich cantons give money to poorer cantons.

gewusst: Because of federalism, the summer holidays do not start at the same time in all cantons.
The municipality with the largest area in Switzerland is Scuol in the Grisons.
Each canton has its own two-letter code on car number plates, such as ZH for Zurich or TI for Ticino.

teile.einleitung: Famous Swiss people are women and men from Switzerland who became famous through their ideas, works or achievements. Some changed the world, for example in science, humanitarian aid or architecture. Others still inspire people today with books or sporting success.
wichtigste: Henry Dunant from Geneva founded the Red Cross and received the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.
Johanna Spyri wrote the stories about “Heidi”.
Albert Einstein developed the special theory of relativity in Bern in 1905.
The world-famous architect Le Corbusier came from La Chaux-de-Fonds.
Roger Federer won 20 Grand Slam singles titles.
Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi wanted children to learn with “head, heart and hand”.
Many famous people have appeared on Swiss banknotes.

abschnitte.text: **Henry Dunant** (1828 to 1910) was a businessman from Geneva. In 1859, after the Battle of Solferino in Italy, he saw thousands of wounded men left without help. He wrote a book about it and inspired the founding of the **Red Cross**, which was created in Geneva in 1863. In 1901, together with the Frenchman Frédéric Passy, he received the very first Nobel Peace Prize.

**Johanna Spyri** (1827 to 1901) grew up in Hirzel in the canton of Zurich. In 1880 her book about **Heidi** was published, an orphan girl who lives with her grandfather on the alp. The story was translated into many languages and made into films several times. Heidi is still one of the best-known characters in children’s literature worldwide.

**Albert Einstein** (1879 to 1955) studied at ETH Zurich and then worked at the patent office in Bern. There in 1905 he published several groundbreaking papers, including the **special theory of relativity**. It shows that time and space do not pass in the same way for everyone. In 1921 he received the Nobel Prize in Physics; his flat in Bern is a museum today.

**Le Corbusier**’s real name was Charles-Édouard Jeanneret, and he was born in La Chaux-de-Fonds in 1887. He is considered one of the most important architects of the 20th century. His concrete buildings with clear shapes and large windows stand in many countries. Several of his works are **UNESCO World Heritage**, and he appeared on the former 10-franc note.

**Roger Federer** was born in Basel in 1981 and is considered one of the best tennis players of all time. He won 20 **Grand Slam** singles titles, 8 of them at Wimbledon alone. For many years he was number 1 in the world rankings. He ended his career in 2022; his foundation supports children’s education in southern Africa.

The Zurich educator **Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi** (1746 to 1827) worked for the education of poor children. He wanted children to learn with “head, heart and hand”, that is with their mind, their feelings and practical work. Other famous people are General Guillaume-Henri Dufour, the sculptor Alberto Giacometti and the adventurer Bertrand Piccard. Piccard flew round the Earth in a balloon in 1999 and in a solar-powered aircraft in 2016.

begriffe.erklaerung: A very famous prize for outstanding achievements, for example for peace or in physics.
Einstein’s theory about the connection between space, time and movement.
The four most important tennis tournaments in the world.
A person who works with upbringing and teaching.

gewusst: At one time Henry Dunant was so poor that he lived in a hospital in Heiden in the Appenzell region.
Albert Einstein developed his famous theory while he was working as a civil servant at the patent office.
Le Corbusier is a pseudonym; his real name was Charles-Édouard Jeanneret.

teile.einleitung: The Schlussgang is the last and most important bout at a Swiss wrestling festival. In it the two best wrestlers of the day meet, and this is usually where the winner of the festival is decided.
wichtigste: The Schlussgang is the last bout of a Swiss wrestling festival.
The two wrestlers with the best results compete against each other in it.
Whoever wins the Schlussgang has a very good chance of winning the festival.
At the Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival, the title of wrestling king is at stake.
A bout can also end in a draw; this is called “gestellt”.
The wrestling takes place in a ring covered with sawdust.

abschnitte.text: **Schwingen** is a kind of wrestling and is considered the Swiss national sport. The wrestlers wear short trousers made of strong cloth, the **wrestling breeches**. They hold on to each other by these. The aim is to put the opponent on his back. The bouts take place in a round ring covered with **sawdust**. After each bout the winner brushes the sawdust off the loser’s back.

At a wrestling festival each wrestler fights several **bouts**. For each bout there are points, depending on whether it was won, lost or drawn. The judges decide the pairings. At the end of the day the two wrestlers with the best results go into the **Schlussgang**. Then all the spectators watch only this one bout.

The biggest wrestling festival is the **Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival**, ESAF for short. It takes place every three years. Whoever has the most points there at the end becomes **wrestling king**. That is why the Schlussgang is especially exciting. If it ends in a draw, another wrestler may end up in the lead.

Swiss wrestling is closely linked with life in the countryside and in the Alps. At wrestling festivals there is often yodelling, alphorn playing and flag throwing. The prizes are traditional: at the ESAF, for example, the winner receives a **Muni**, that is a bull. **Fairness** is important too: after the bout the wrestlers shake hands.

gewusst: At the end of a bout the winner brushes the sawdust off the loser’s back as a sign of respect.
At the Federal festival, tens of thousands of people watch in a huge arena.

teile.einleitung: Cultural heritage includes not only castles and churches but also customs, festivals and crafts. These living traditions are called intangible cultural heritage. UNESCO keeps a list of them, which also includes Swiss traditions.
wichtigste: Intangible cultural heritage means customs, knowledge and skills that you cannot touch.
UNESCO adopted a convention on it in 2003.
Switzerland joined this convention in 2008.
The Basel Fasnacht was added to the UNESCO list in 2017.
The Confederation keeps its own list of living traditions in Switzerland.
The aim is for the traditions to be passed on.

abschnitte.text: **Intangible** means that you cannot touch something. This refers to **customs**, festivals, music, dances, stories and **crafts**. They stay alive because people practise them and pass them on to younger people. A building stays standing even if nobody looks at it. A custom, on the other hand, disappears if nobody keeps it up any more.

**UNESCO** is a United Nations organisation for education, science and culture. In 2003 it adopted a **convention** to protect intangible cultural heritage. Countries can propose traditions, which are then added to a worldwide list. Switzerland joined the convention in **2008**. Being added is a recognition, not a competition.

In **2017** the **Basel Fasnacht** was added to the list, with the Morgestraich, Cliquen, drums, piccolos and Schnitzelbänke, the satirical verses. Other entries followed later, some together with neighbouring countries. These include managing **avalanche risk**, which Switzerland submitted with Austria, and the **craft of watchmaking**, together with France. **Alpinism** is also on the list.

The Confederation also keeps its own **list of living traditions in Switzerland**. It includes many customs from all parts of the country. On it are, for example, the **driving of cattle up to the alpine pastures**, **yodelling**, Swiss wrestling and many Fasnacht customs. The list is looked after by the **Federal Office of Culture** together with the cantons and added to from time to time.

gewusst: Switzerland’s list also includes skills, such as how to build dry stone walls.
As well as intangible cultural heritage, there is UNESCO World Heritage, which includes the old town of Bern, for example.

teile.einleitung: The National Council is the large chamber of the Swiss parliament. Its 200 members represent the people and are elected every four years. Together with the Council of States it forms the Federal Assembly, which meets in the Federal Palace in Bern.
wichtigste: The National Council has 200 members.
The number of seats a canton has depends on its population.
Each canton has at least one seat in the National Council.
The canton of Zurich has the most members of the National Council.
The National Council meets in the Federal Palace in Bern.
Parliament holds four regular sessions a year.
Elections take place every four years in October.

abschnitte.text: The **National Council** is one of the two chambers of the Federal Assembly; the other is the **Council of States**. Both chambers have equal rights and must agree to a law for it to apply. The National Council is also called the people’s chamber because it represents the population. The Council of States, on the other hand, represents the cantons. This two-chamber system was introduced in 1848 on the model of the USA.

abschnitte.titel: How the seats are shared out
abschnitte.text: The 200 seats are shared out among the cantons according to their **population**. The more people live in a canton, the more seats it has. The canton of Zurich has the most, with 36 seats (as of 2023). Each canton has at least one seat, for example Uri, Glarus or Appenzell Innerrhoden.

The National Council is elected by the people every four years, most recently in October 2023. In most cantons **proportional representation** applies, so the seats are shared out according to the parties’ share of the vote. Voters can cross out names on a list, mix different parties or write people down twice. In cantons with only one seat, the person with the most votes wins.

Parliament meets four times a year for a **session**: in spring, summer, autumn and winter. A session normally lasts three weeks. In between, the members work in **committees**, which prepare the business. Most members of parliament also have another job; this is called a militia parliament.

The National Council meets in the National Council chamber of the **Federal Palace** in Bern, which was opened in 1902. Every year it elects a new president. This person chairs the sittings and is formally considered the highest-ranking Swiss citizen. The sittings are public; you can follow them from the gallery or on the internet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sitting period during which parliament meets.
An election in which the seats are shared out among the parties according to their share of the vote.
A small group of members of parliament who prepare a topic in detail.
A parliament whose members do politics alongside their job.

gewusst: In 1971 the first women were elected to the National Council.
A large mural in the National Council chamber shows the Rütli meadow on Lake Lucerne.
Votes in the National Council are taken electronically at the press of a button, and the results appear on large display boards.

teile.einleitung: The Unspunnen Festival is a big festival of Swiss folk culture in Interlaken in the Bernese Oberland. It is famous above all for the Unspunnen Stone, a heavy stone that athletes throw as far as possible.
wichtigste: The Unspunnen Festival takes place in Interlaken.
The first festival was held in 1805.
The Unspunnen Stone weighs about 83.5 kilograms.
In stone putting you try to throw the stone as far as possible.
Swiss wrestling, yodelling, alphorn playing and traditional costumes are also part of the festival.
The festival only takes place at fairly long intervals.

abschnitte.titel: A festival with a long history
abschnitte.text: The first **Unspunnen Festival** took place in 1805 and a second in 1808. It is named after the **ruined Unspunnen Castle** near Interlaken. The festival was meant to bring together people from town and country. At that time Switzerland was politically unsettled. Later the festival was revived and since then has taken place at irregular, usually fairly long intervals.

The **Unspunnen Stone** is the best-known stone in Switzerland. It weighs about **83.5 kilograms**. In **stone putting**, the athlete picks up the stone, takes a short run-up and pushes it forwards with one arm. What is measured is how far it flies. Because the stone is so heavy, distances of a few metres are already a great achievement.

abschnitte.titel: Folk culture from all over Switzerland
abschnitte.text: The festival is not only about strength. There is **Swiss wrestling**, yodelling, alphorn playing and flag throwing. Many visitors wear **traditional costumes** from their region. Groups from all parts of the country show their customs. This makes the Unspunnen Festival a showcase of Swiss folk culture.

The original stone has an eventful history. In **1984** it was stolen. Behind this were activists fighting for the independence of the Jura from the canton of Bern. It only reappeared many years later. This story has made the stone even more famous.

gewusst: Interlaken lies between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz, which is where the name comes from: “between the lakes”.
Besides the Unspunnen Stone, there are also lighter stones in stone putting for other categories.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss cross is a white cross with four arms of equal length on a red background. It is the most important symbol of Switzerland and appears on its flag and its coat of arms. All over the world people recognise Switzerland by it at once.
wichtigste: The Swiss cross has 4 arms of equal length.
On the Swiss flag the white cross is in the middle of a red square.
The Swiss flag is square, which is very rare in the world.
The Red Cross emblem looks like the Swiss flag with the colours reversed.
A Swiss cross on a product often shows that it comes from Switzerland.
A law sets out who may use the Swiss cross.
Since 1848 the cross has been the official sign of the federal state.

abschnitte.text: The **Swiss cross** is a free-standing white cross on a red background. Its four arms are the same length and each is one sixth longer than it is wide. On the **Swiss flag** the cross is exactly in the middle. The flag is square; only the Vatican also has a square national flag. On ships Switzerland uses a rectangular flag.

The cross originally comes from the flag of the canton of **Schwyz**, which was red and showed a small white cross in one corner. As early as the Middle Ages, Confederate warriors sewed white crosses onto their clothing as a **field sign**. This let them recognise each other in battle. With the founding of the federal state in 1848, the white cross on a red background became the official coat of arms of Switzerland.

The Red Cross was founded in Geneva in 1863. In honour of Switzerland, the Swiss flag with the **colours reversed**, that is a red cross on a white background, was chosen as its protective emblem. In war this emblem protects the wounded, medics and hospitals. It may only be used by authorised organisations.

Many companies use the Swiss cross on their products, because “Made in Switzerland” stands for quality. So that the cross is not misused, strict rules called **Swissness** have applied since 2017. For food, for example, at least 80 per cent of the raw materials must come from Switzerland. For industrial products, at least 60 per cent of the manufacturing costs must arise in Switzerland.

You can see the Swiss cross on buildings, on sports shirts, on pocket knives and on Swiss aircraft. On 1 August many people decorate their houses with Swiss flags. At sporting events fans paint the cross on their cheeks. The **coat of arms** of Switzerland also shows the white cross, but on a red shield.

begriffe.erklaerung: A piece of cloth with colours and symbols that stands for a country.
A symbol on a shield that represents a country, a canton or a family.
A sign of recognition by which soldiers recognised each other in battle.
Rules on when a product may be described as Swiss.

gewusst: Switzerland and the Vatican are the only countries with a square national flag.
The Red Cross emblem is a tribute to Switzerland, where the organisation was founded.
The Swiss cross is protected by its own law, the Coat of Arms Protection Act.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss franc is the currency of Switzerland and Liechtenstein. One franc is made up of 100 centimes, called Rappen in German. It is considered a particularly stable and safe currency around the world.
wichtigste: One franc has 100 centimes (Rappen).
The abbreviation is CHF, after the Latin name of the country, Confoederatio Helvetica.
The largest banknote is the 1000-franc note.
The 50-franc note is green.
2 francs and 50 centimes make 250 centimes.
The banknotes are issued by the Swiss National Bank.
The franc has been Switzerland’s common currency since 1850.

abschnitte.text: The **franc** is the money people pay with in Switzerland. It is divided into 100 **Rappen**; in French they are called centimes. The international abbreviation is **CHF**; the C and H stand for Confoederatio Helvetica. In the Principality of Liechtenstein people also pay with Swiss francs.

There are banknotes of 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs. Each has its own colour: 10 yellow, 20 red, 50 green, 100 blue, 200 brown and 1000 purple. The current ninth series was introduced from 2016 to 2019 and shows “the many facets of Switzerland”, with a hand and a globe as recurring motifs. Modern **security features** such as transparent windows and holograms protect against forgeries.

There are coins of 5, 10 and 20 centimes and of ½, 1, 2 and 5 francs. The 5-franc coin is popularly called the **Fünfliber**. The franc coins show the standing Helvetia, a woman who symbolises Switzerland. The coins are minted by **Swissmint** in Bern. The 1-centime coin was abolished in 2007 because it was hardly used any more.

The **Swiss National Bank** (SNB) was founded in 1907 and is responsible for the franc. It issues the banknotes and makes sure that prices stay stable. It has offices in Bern and Zurich. Because the franc is considered safe, people from all over the world buy it, especially in times of crisis; that is why it is called a safe haven.

Before the federal state existed, many cantons had their own money, and there were dozens of different coins. With the Coinage Act of 1850, the franc became the single currency of the whole of Switzerland. The National Bank issued the first uniform banknotes from 1907. Unlike many neighbouring countries, Switzerland has not introduced the euro.

If you calculate with francs and centimes, you can turn everything into centimes. For example, 2 francs and 50 centimes make 250 centimes. At the till, amounts are rounded to 5 centimes because there are no smaller coins any more. Prices are usually written like this: Fr. 2.50 or CHF 2.50.

begriffe.erklaerung: The money that is legal tender in a country.
The hundredth part of a franc (a centime).
The popular name for the 5-franc coin.
The state’s bank, which issues the money and makes sure prices are stable.
A special feature on banknotes that makes forgeries harder.

gewusst: The 1000-franc note is one of the most valuable banknotes in the world.
Swiss banknotes are printed in Zurich by the company Orell Füssli.
The name of the National Bank appears on every banknote in all four national languages.
